item.title: Modi quiere que India lidere la era de la IA, pero los ciudadanos se oponen
item.description: Las vistas desde el piso del ingeniero indio Tushar Shetty en Bombay reflejan una tensión que se está viviendo en todo el mundo, a medida que el auge de la inteligencia artificial impulsa una oleada sin precedentes de construcción de centros de datos.
item.dc:creator: Vibhuti Sharma, Munsif Vengattil, Aditya Kalra
item.content:encoded: Las vistas desde el piso del ingeniero indio Tushar Shetty en Bombay reflejan una tensión que se está viviendo en todo el mundo, a medida que el auge de la inteligencia artificial impulsa una oleada sin precedentes de construcción de centros de datos. Lo que antes era una frondosa zona verde desde la ventana de su piso en la planta 21 es ahora una cicatriz de tierra roja donde se talaron los árboles para dar paso a unas instalaciones de Amazon que forman parte de la inversión prevista por el gigante tecnológico de 21.000 millones de dólares en infraestructura de IA en India de aquí a 2030. "No habría comprado la casa si lo hubiera sabido", afirma este hombre de 46 años, lamentando una compra realizada hace apenas cinco meses. Desde los suburbios de Virginia hasta las afueras de Ámsterdam y Dublín, los residentes se rebelan cada vez más contra la expansión de los centros de datos de IA, quejándose del ruido, el aumento del consumo eléctrico, el estrés hídrico y la industrialización de los barrios residenciales. Esa resistencia está ganando terreno en India, donde Amazon, Google y Microsoft están invirtiendo miles de millones en instalaciones que impulsan la ambición del primer ministro Narendra Modi de albergar "todos los datos del mundo", desde Maharashtra, al oeste, hasta Andhra Pradesh, al sur. Incapaz por ahora de igualar los modelos pioneros que surgen de EEUU y China, India está siguiendo un camino diferente, apostando por que el dominio de la infraestructura física de la IA pueda resultar igual de valioso. Esta estrategia constituye el núcleo del argumento de inversión de Modi, en un momento en que la trastienda del mundo pierde su atractivo, aunque dicha ambición choca con las preocupaciones por la escasez de recursos y por las comunidades que conviven con las infraestructuras que impulsan la economía digital. India posee el 4% del agua dulce del mundo para el 18% de su población, y los centros de datos se están concentrando en ciudades que ya sufren escasez de este recurso. S&P Global estima que entre el 60% y el 80% de los centros de datos indios podrían enfrentarse a un grave estrés hídrico durante esta década. En 2025, los centros de datos consumieron unos 150.000 millones de litros de agua, una cifra que, según la consultora Mordor Intelligence, se duplicará con creces de aquí a 2030. El proyecto de Amazon cerca de Bombay se está convirtiendo en uno de los puntos más conflictivos de India. Las entrevistas de Reuters con más de dos decenas de residentes y un análisis de la correspondencia oficial revelan una creciente preocupación por que el proyecto suponga una carga para el suministro local de electricidad y agua y genere un ruido perjudicial para la salud, especialmente para los niños y las personas mayores. Amazon y las autoridades locales han defendido enérgicamente el proyecto, afirmando que no supondrá una carga para los servicios públicos, ya que el agua y la electricidad procederán de fuentes específicas. No obstante, la controversia ha desencadenado protestas callejeras y ha arrastrado a políticos de la oposición a la contienda. El Gobierno de Modi también ha salido en defensa del proyecto, promocionando los centros de datos en internet como "los motores invisibles que impulsan la vida digital de India" y argumentando que las tecnologías modernas utilizan el agua y la electricidad de forma más eficiente. El Ministerio de Electrónica y Tecnología de la Información, la Oficina del primer ministro y la oficina del ministro principal de Maharashtra no respondieron a las solicitudes de comentarios. El 8 de septiembre, cientos de vecinos, entre ellos personas mayores, se reunieron junto al emplazamiento con pancartas en las que se leía "Los centros de datos son vampiros energéticos". Quieren que el proyecto se traslade a otro lugar. "Si se detiene el centro de datos, nos quedaremos… Si sigue adelante, nos iremos", afirmó Vasudha Shetty, de 62 años, que compró un piso cerca de las instalaciones previstas, de unas 22 hectáreas, pero que quiere dar prioridad a una jubilación tranquila.

item.title: Agentes del ICE disparan a un hombre en Nueva York delante de un niño, según el alcalde
item.description: Agentes de inmigración estadounidenses dispararon e hirieron el jueves a un hombre que se encontraba en su vehículo, en presencia de un niño, en el barrio de Marble Hill de la ciudad de Nueva York, según el alcalde, la policía municipal y testigos presenciales.
item.dc:creator: Julia Harte, Kristina Cooke
item.content:encoded: Agentes de inmigración estadounidenses dispararon e hirieron el jueves a un hombre que se encontraba en su vehículo, en presencia de un niño, en el barrio de Marble Hill de la ciudad de Nueva York, según el alcalde, la policía municipal y testigos presenciales. Los agentes federales de inmigración han disparado al menos a 21 personas desde que el presidente republicano Donald Trump volvió al cargo, siete de las cuales murieron, lo que ha desencadenado protestas en todo Estados Unidos. Los críticos sostienen que la campaña de Trump para intensificar las deportaciones ha provocado un número cada vez mayor de enfrentamientos violentos, y acusan al Gobierno de negarse a rendir cuentas por los agentes implicados. Trump ha afirmado que hay que deportar a muchos migrantes, a los que culpa, a menudo en términos generales, de fraudes financieros y delitos violentos. "Los primeros reportes indican que los agentes rodearon (al hombre) y a un niño de 5 años en su automóvil antes de disparar varias ráfagas", dijo el alcalde de Nueva York, Zohran Mamdani, en un comunicado. "He estado hablando por teléfono con el presidente Trump y con el secretario de Seguridad Nacional, Mullin, negociando la puesta en libertad del hombre al que dispararon los agentes del ICE. Esas negociaciones no tuvieron éxito", declaró Mamdani en una rueda de prensa a última hora de la tarde neoyorquina. Dijo que exigió al Gobierno de Trump que el ICE detuviera sus acciones de control en la ciudad de Nueva York. "Estas acciones están haciendo que la ciudad sea menos segura", dijo Mamdani. "Esta ciudad quiere que el ICE se vaya. Queremos que el ICE se vaya de nuestra ciudad, que el ICE se vaya de nuestras escuelas, que el ICE se vaya de nuestros hospitales, que el ICE se vaya de nuestras calles, que el ICE se aleje de nuestros niños". El alcalde dijo que el niño que se encontraba en el vehículo resultó ileso. La comisaria de la Policía de Nueva York, Jessica Tisch, indicó que la policía de Nueva York ha localizado al niño con un familiar tras realizar una visita de control. El Departamento de Seguridad Nacional, organismo del que depende el ICE, dijo en un comunicado que los agentes del ICE estaban llevando a cabo una "operación de aplicación selectiva de la ley" en el Bronx, Nueva York, para detener a un hombre de República Dominicana con antecedentes penales. El hombre, identificado como un individuo de 28 años, había sido detenido en dos ocasiones en la ciudad de Nueva York, en 2023 y 2025, según la comisaria del NYPD, Tisch. "Durante el incidente, un agente del ICE disparó su arma y el extranjero ilegal con antecedentes penales resultó herido", dijo el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional, que añadió que los agentes del ICE le prestaron asistencia inmediata. "El individuo se encuentra con vida y en un hospital local". El tiroteo tuvo lugar alrededor de las 16:00 hora local (2000 GMT), según el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional. Pedro Almarez, que trabaja en un restaurante cercano al lugar del tiroteo, afirmó que oyó disparos y salió a la calle, donde vio a varios agentes vestidos con el uniforme del ICE en el lugar de los hechos. "Había muchos agentes del ICE, tres o cuatro vehículos", explicó Almarez a Reuters por teléfono. Dijo que los agentes de la Policía de Nueva York llegaron unos 10 minutos más tarde. Según él, el hombre no fue sacado de su automóvil hasta que llegó una ambulancia. En el lugar del tiroteo, donde la policía colocó cinta amarilla de escena del crimen para acordonar la cuadra, una mujer que se encontraba en un balcón con vistas a la zona dijo a los agentes que se estaban "llevando" a sus "hijos", según un testigo de Reuters.

item.title: Le secteur du luxe freiné davantage par des mesures fiscales en Chine
item.description: Le tour de vis enclenché par la Chine pour lutter contre l'évasion fiscale des plus fortunés est devenu un motif supplémentaire d'inquiétude pour les enseignes de luxe, lesquelles font déjà face aux répercussions de la guerre en Iran et à un ralentissement de la consommation aux Etats-Unis.
item.dc:creator: Tassilo Hummel, Sophie Yu
item.content:encoded: Le tour de vis enclenché par la Chine pour lutter contre l'évasion fiscale des plus fortunés est devenu un motif supplémentaire d'inquiétude pour les enseignes de luxe, lesquelles font déjà face aux répercussions de la guerre en Iran et à un ralentissement de la consommation aux Etats-Unis. Cette situation devrait peser sur les résultats trimestriels du secteur, qui seront communiqués à partir de la semaine prochaine, et renforcer la crainte que le luxe, au ralenti depuis trois ans, ne retrouvera pas facilement son lustre d'auparavant. Depuis le début de l'année, les actions de LVMH (LVMH.PA) et de Hermes (HRMS.PA) ont chuté d'environ 40% pour s'établir à des creux de plusieurs années. Kering (PRTP.PA) , propriétaire de la marque Gucci, a pour sa part cédé 29%, illustrant le pessimisme accru des investisseurs à propos du secteur du luxe, qui pèse 350 milliards de dollars. En Chine, la nouvelle réglementation fiscale mise en place par Pékin exige de ceux utilisant des comptes offshore qu'ils déclarent ces actifs avant le 22 octobre et versent des arriérés d'impôts à hauteur de 20%. Cela laisse entrevoir un possible ralentissement des dépenses dans l'un des marchés cruciaux du luxe - les consommateurs chinois représentent environ un cinquième des achats mondiaux du secteur, même si la demande locale a nettement reculé depuis la crise du COVID. "Jusqu'à la date butoir pour payer cet impôt, certains pourraient être confrontés à des problèmes de liquidités", a commenté Alexis Bonhomme, directeur de la firme de conseil du luxe Trinity Asia, basée à Shanghaï, notant que les Chinois les plus fortunés s'étaient auparavant montrés plus résilients que les consommateurs de la classe moyenne, affectés par la crise prolongée du secteur immobilier. "Cela ne veut pas dire qu'ils ne vont pas effectuer des achats, mais dans l'immédiat, le moral n'y est pas", a-t-il ajouté. Dans une note, les analystes de Bernstein ont déclaré que les données des centres commerciaux en Chine continentale indiquaient une "nette décélération de la croissance". LVMH donnera lundi le coup d'envoi des résultats du secteur du luxe; les analystes s'attendent à une hausse de 1% sur un an des ventes trimestrielles du groupe français. Kering et Hermes publieront leurs résultats le 22 octobre. Kering a déjà averti sur les résultats de Gucci, ce qui a déclenché plusieurs recommandations à la baisse pour son titre.

item.title: India's Aditya Birla unit seeks $1.5 billion in rupee loans to buy Shell arm Solenergi, bankers say
item.description: India's Aditya Birla Renewables is seeking $1.5 billion in rupee-denominated loans to fund the acquisition of Shell Plc's Indian renewable energy arm and avoid a costlier bridge debt, three bankers aware of the discussions said.
item.dc:creator: Khushi Malhotra
item.content:encoded: India's Aditya Birla Renewables is seeking $1.5 billion in rupee-denominated loans to fund the acquisition of Shell Plc's Indian renewable energy arm and avoid a costlier bridge debt, three bankers aware of the discussions said. The renewable-energy arm of Aditya Birla Group agreed in July to acquire Solenergi Power, a Shell Plc unit that includes the Sprng Energy group companies, for $1.8 billion. The Aditya Birla Group firm had earlier secured a $1.6 billion bridge loan commitment from MUFG Bank to fund the acquisition, two bankers said. The bankers declined to be identified as they are not authorised to speak to the media. A spokesperson for Aditya Birla Renewables (ABRen) did not respond to Reuters queries sent by email on Thursday. The Indian company is now looking to raise longer-term rupee-denominated loans at the project level to avoid the bridge facility, the three bankers cited above said. Bridge financing is usually intended as interim funding and comes at a higher cost, while longer-term project financing is backed by assets and reduces the cost of funding. The tenor of the loans is expected to be around 80% of the project's lifecycle, one of the bankers said. It will likely be split across 17-20 special purpose vehicles holding individual projects, including some that are already operational and the balance under construction, one of the bankers cited above said. ABRen is not immediately required to make payment to Shell because the transaction is yet to close, giving it time to finalise the financing structure. The company has reached out to multiple Indian banks, including the State Bank of India and HDFC Bank, for the loans, the bankers added. MUFG, SBI and HDFC Bank did not reply to requests for comment.

item.title: POINT MARCHÉS L'Europe vue dans le vert, accalmie sur le pétrole et les rendements (actualisé)
item.description: Les principales Bourses européennes sont attendues sur un rebond vendredi à l'ouverture, portées par la baisse des cours du pétrole et une accalmie sur le marché obligataire, même si la volatilité reste élevée en raison des craintes budgétaires dans des pays comme la France.
item.dc:creator: Diana Mandia
item.content:encoded: Les principales Bourses européennes sont attendues sur un rebond vendredi à l'ouverture, portées par la baisse des cours du pétrole et une accalmie sur le marché obligataire, même si la volatilité reste élevée en raison des craintes budgétaires dans des pays comme la France. Les contrats à terme sur indices suggèrent une ouverture en hausse de 0,71% pour le CAC 40 parisien (.FCHI) , de 0,67% pour le Dax à Francfort (.GDAXI) , de 0,8% pour le FTSE à Londres (.FTSE) et de 0,62% pour le Stoxx 600 (.STOXX) . Les cours du pétrole reculent légèrement vendredi après que le président américain Donald Trump [USN:L8N45U1RL TEXT:"a déclaré"] la veille que les Etats-Unis ne lanceraient pas d'attaque contre l'Iran d'ici aux élections de mi-mandat prévues début novembre, ajoutant que Washington avait des discussions "productives" avec Téhéran. Ces propos ont contribué à apaiser les prix du brut, alors même que le marché observait avec inquiétude l'augmentation des attaques contre les navires transitant par le détroit d'Ormuz et les tensions croissantes en Arabie saoudite, cible d'une nouvelle série d'attaques de la part des Houthis du Yémen, alliés de l'Iran. Cela permet également d'apaiser la dernière flambée des rendements de la dette souveraine, en proie à une forte agitation due aux anticipations d'une politique monétaire plus ferme contre l'inflation, mais aussi aux doutes que suscite chez les opérateurs l'évolution budgétaire de certains pays. En France, notamment, le rendement de l'OAT à dix ans se maintient près de son plus haut niveau depuis 24 ans, atteint vendredi dernier, et son écart par rapport à l'obligation allemande de même échéance se situe à un pic depuis la crise de la zone euro de 2011-2012. Les investisseurs se montrent sceptiques face à un projet de budget pour 2027 dont l'issue est incertaine, ainsi qu'à l'égard de la capacité de la deuxième économie de la zone euro à réduire son déficit à l'approche de l'élection présidentielle du printemps prochain. "Il est essentiel que tous les États membres, et en particulier ceux qui affichent des déficits ou des dettes élevés, mènent des politiques budgétaires prudentes. De ce point de vue, l'élaboration d'un budget solide pour l'année prochaine sera importante pour garantir cette prévisibilité et cette crédibilité, et pour rassurer les marchés. Je suis en contact avec le ministre [français des Finances] Lescure à ce sujet" a déclaré jeudi lors d'une conférence de presse le commissaire européen à l'Économie, Valdis Dombrovskis. Le rendement des bons du Trésor américain recule vendredi après la forte demande enregistrée lors d'une adjudication d'obligations à 30 ans ; toutefois, le gestionnaire d'actifs Pimco, cité par le Financial Times, a indiqué qu'il pourrait atteindre 6% pour la première fois depuis l'année 2000. Les craintes concernant l'endettement élevé des entreprises technologiques et les rendements qu'il génère refont en outre surface, ce qui pèse ce vendredi sur les marchés asiatiques, dans le sillage de Wall Street la veille. Selon le Financial Times, le chiffre d'affaires annualisé de la start-up spécialisée dans l'intelligence artificielle OpenAI est inférieur de 20 milliards de dollars à ce que l'entreprise avait initialement anticipé. Une nouvelle vague massive de levées de fonds semble par ailleurs se profiler chez SpaceX (SPCX.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) et Oracle (ORCL.N) , au moment même où le financement devient plus coûteux. LES VALEURS A SUIVRE : [USN:L8N45U1Q4] A WALL STREET La Bourse de New York a fini en ordre dispersé jeudi, seul le Dow Jones marquant une petite hausse, alors que les prix du pétrole ont bondi en raison d'attaques autour du détroit d'Ormuz, alimentant les craintes sur l'inflation et la hausse des taux d'intérêt. L'indice Dow Jones (.DJI) a gagné 0,10%, le S&P-500 (.SPX) , plus large, a perdu 0,47%, et le Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) a reculé de son côté de 1,25%. Le compartiment des fabricants de puces (.SOX) a reculé de 3,4% les informations sur le chiffre d'affaires annualisé d'OpenAI. L'opérateur australien de centres de données Firmus, soutenu par Nvidia (NVDA.O) , a par ailleurs suspendu son introduction en Bourse, invoquant la volatilité et les conditions du marché, et a indiqué qu'il opterait plutôt pour une levée de fonds privée. Dans le reste de l'actualité des entreprises, les États-Unis ont suspendu Microsoft (MSFT.O) , les principaux prestataires de services informatiques et l'éditeur de logiciels Adobe (ADBE.O) d'un programme de visas H-1B pour travailleurs qualifiés, tout en ouvrant des enquêtes sur neuf universités, dans le cadre d'une campagne qui, selon les autorités, vise à lutter contre la fraude et à protéger les emplois américains. EN ASIE L'indice Nikkei (.N225) de la Bourse de Tokyo a fini en légère baisse (-0,02%), les investisseurs faisant preuve de prudence face aux risques liés à l'IA et à la situation du marché obligataire, même s'il réduit ses pertes en fin de séance. SoftBank (9984.T) , qui selon le Financial Times cherche à lever jusqu'à 100 milliards de dollars auprès d'investisseurs du Golfe afin de financer une nouvelle vague d'investissements dans l'IA, a perdu près de 4%. En Chine, l'indice CSI 300 (.CSI300) des grandes capitalisations avance de 0,35% et le SSE Composite (.SSEC) de Shanghaï 0,22%. La Bourse de Hong Kong (.HSI) gagne 0,56%. TAUX / CHANGES Le rendement des Treasuries à dix ans gagne 1,3 point de base à 5,2441%, tandis que celui du titre à deux ans avance légèrement à 4,7680%. Christopher Waller, gouverneur de la Réserve fédérale américaine (Fed), a dit qu'il existe une "certaine souplesse" quant au rythme du resserrement monétaire envisagé par l'institution, qui a relevé ses taux en septembre pour la première fois en plus de trois ans. Malgré une inflation bien au-dessus de sa cible, les investisseurs estiment que la banque centrale attendra le mois de décembre pour relever ses coûts d'emprunt pour la deuxième fois cette année. Dans la zone euro, le rendement du Bund allemand à dix ans recule de 3,6 points de base à 3,4576%, tandis que celui du titre à deux ans perd 3,1 points de base à 3,0537%. En France, le rendement de l'OAT à dix ans abandonne 6,8 points de base à 4,8198%, et son "spread" avec son homologue allemand s'établit à 135 points de base dans les premiers échanges de la séance. Outre les craintes budgétaires qui devraient persister, [USN:L6N45U0QP TEXT:"les économistes"] interrogés par Reuters estiment que la Banque centrale européenne (BCE) laissera son taux de dépôt inchangé ce mois-ci avant de le relever en décembre. Sur le marché des changes, le dollar perd 0,10% face à un panier de devises de référence (.DXY) , ce qui permet à l'euro de se redresser légèrement après que les craintes liées aux finances publiques l'ont fait chuter lundi dernier à son plus bas niveau depuis 17 mois. La monnaie européenne gagne 0,16% à 1,1227 dollar . PÉTROLE Le Brent perd 0,96% à 103,28 dollars le baril et le brut léger américain (West Texas Intermediate, WTI) 0,87% à 90,69 dollars. La Chine s'apprête par ailleurs à reprendre ses exportations de carburants raffinés en octobre, après une brève interruption pendant la "Golden Week", une mesure qui devrait contribuer à détendre les marchés du diesel, de l'essence et du kérosène, ont déclaré vendredi quatre opérateurs proches du dossier. item.title: Inside the deadlock at the world's top climate science body
item.description: The decision was expected to take minutes. But after nearly three years of debate, members of the world’s leading authority on climate change still can’t agree on a timeline to publish its next review of the latest science on the warming planet.
item.dc:creator: Kate Abnett, Sudarshan Varadhan
item.content:encoded: The decision was expected to take minutes. But after nearly three years of debate, members of the world’s leading authority on climate change still can’t agree on a timeline to publish its next review of the latest science on the warming planet. Such assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) have informed every major United Nations climate agreement for three decades. But the impasse over publication dates could leave countries to decide the next phase of action without consensus on critical issues – including the extent to which some global warming might be reversible – according to interviews with more than a dozen current and former IPCC scientists, government negotiators and meeting observers. The dispute reflects deep rifts between wealthy industrialized nations, major emerging economies and poorer nations over how to respond to rapidly warming temperatures and how much of that burden should be shouldered by different countries. On Monday, representatives from the IPCC’s 195 member states will convene in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia's capital, for a plenary meeting many see as the last chance to agree publication dates falling before UN climate talks in November 2028. That’s when governments are due to assess progress toward goals set out in the landmark agreement reached in Paris in 2015. The UN Environment Programme has said repeatedly that global efforts to limit warming [USN:L1N44U06P TEXT:"are falling short"] and that faster emissions cuts are needed to avoid more extreme weather and climate-related disasters. Scientists have said climate change fueled wildfires that surged across Europe this summer and likely played a role in landslides and flash floods that killed hundreds in Nepal and China’s Tibet. The possibility the IPCC’s reports might not be ready in time for the 2028 climate talks has alarmed a coalition of countries pushing for more robust action. Those discussions are intended to guide decisions on climate financing and national targets to bring down greenhouse gas emissions. “Access to the latest and best available science … enables a just, equitable, evidence-based approach to addressing the greatest challenge of our time, rather than one driven by those whose entrenched interests are at odds with reducing greenhouse gases,” the High Ambition Coalition said in a statement due to be published on Friday. The statement, seen by Reuters, is signed by more than 30 countries, including European, Latin American and small-island states. The IPCC does not conduct original research. But its reviews of the world’s existing knowledge on climate change – published every five to seven years – carry weight with governments because they are written by hundreds of international experts and approved by every member state. IPCC findings contributed to a commitment in the Paris Agreement to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Its reports are also used by governments to plan their responses to climate change and have been cited in international court rulings. Countries including India, Kenya, Saudi Arabia, Russia and China are pressing for more time to prepare the IPCC’s next reports to ensure scientists from less-resourced countries can make meaningful contributions. Some struggle to publish new research in time to be included or to take time off from their regular jobs for unpaid IPCC work, they say. “If you have a process that goes very quickly … it wouldn't be inclusive,” said Joyce Kimutai, a climate scientist who represents Kenya at the IPCC. ‘THE ELEPHANT IN THE ROOM’ The deadlock – unprecedented in the IPCC’s history – comes as the organization faces increasing pressure from governments critical of climate policies they say hurt industrial competitiveness or restrict the ability of emerging economies to use cheaper, more polluting fuels to meet development needs. The United States, the IPCC’s biggest funder, [USN:L1N3Y903Y TEXT:"quit the organization"] in January. The IPCC will publish three key reports: one on the extent and causes of climate change, another on vulnerabilities and how countries can adapt, and a third on options to avoid warming getting worse. Scientists chairing groups preparing the reports have proposed a work plan that would see all three approved by September 2028. Robert Vautard, a French co-chair, said the proposal was based on the anticipated workload rather than the timing of the 2028 UN summit. Report timelines are typically approved in "a matter of minutes," he added. Opponents of the chairs’ proposal want the second and third reports pushed into 2029, saying the timeline is too short to analyze thousands of studies, agree wording and complete expert and government reviews. The dispute is sowing discord and distrust in an organization intended to help countries bridge divides by providing a scientific basis for climate negotiations. Observers at five previous IPCC meetings described days of contentious debate. Participants have traded accusations of politicizing the IPCC’s work. Some pushing to publish before the 2028 summit note that major oil-producing nations are among the most vocal advocates for more time, accusing them of trying to avoid pressure to reduce carbon dioxide emissions more quickly. “The elephant in the room is the politics,” said Lisa Schipper, an IPCC editor from Sweden. Some countries, she said, are using the debate as a “stalling tactic.” Russia’s economy ministry said framing the debate as a confrontation with oil producers was a “deliberate misrepresentation.” Attempts to synchronize the assessment cycle with UN negotiations “raise serious questions about preserving the IPCC's independent nature,” the ministry said. “In such circumstances, there is a risk that scientific assessments could be used to advance a predetermined climate policy agenda.” Thiagarajan Jayaraman, a scientist who represents India at the IPCC, said it was “short-sighted” to suggest the value of the body’s work rests solely on contributing to the 2028 UN talks. Representatives from Saudi Arabia and China have made similar arguments at previous meetings. Their governments did not respond to questions for this article. EQUITY AND INCLUSIVITY Developing countries have long argued their perspectives are not sufficiently reflected in IPCC reports because they do not have enough experts involved and because their researchers have fewer resources to publish peer-reviewed studies. The result, Thiagarajan said, is that issues of "equity and inclusivity” are in some instances “simply ducked.” He takes issue, for example, with what he says is a lack of consideration of wealthy countries’ historical contributions to global warming and poorer nations’ development needs in models the IPCC uses to evaluate how much temperatures might rise under different emissions scenarios. India argues countries that got rich through centuries of fossil fuel use should make the biggest emissions cuts. Some industrialized nations want major emerging economies such as India and China, now among the world’s biggest emitters, to also make ambitious cuts. The IPCC says it is taking steps to make assessments more inclusive. Just over half the lead authors and editors selected for the next review are from developing economies or ones in transition. The next reports will for the first time include chapters on climate finance and addressing irreversible harm inflicted on some countries, IPCC Chair Jim Skea said in June, issues important to many developing nations. Jozef Pecho, a climatologist at GoSpace Labs in Slovakia who uses IPCC reports in his work, said he feared “the room for cherry picking and distorting science would grow” if governments don’t have an updated assessment for the 2028 UN talks. Countries pushing for that timeline at the IPCC say negotiators would otherwise have to rely on reports published in 2021-22. Much has changed since then. In 2024, global temperatures [USN:L4N3O50P3 TEXT:"averaged more than 1.5 C"] above pre-industrial levels for the first time. The next reports will attempt to fill knowledge gaps about the overshoot, including the potential consequences of interventions to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Joeri Rogelj, an IPCC author from Belgium, said there was no use in writing such assessments if they aren’t available when policy makers can use them. “The importance of the IPCC … is that these authoritative assessments of science are being used,” he said.

item.content:encoded: Der österreichische Öl-, Gas- und Chemiekonzern OMV (OMVV.VI) bekommt im dritten Quartal ausbleibende Rohölverladungen im Nahen Osten zu spüren. Wie aus dem am Freitag veröffentlichten Trading Update des Konzerns hervorgeht, dürfte dies das operative Ergebnis vor Sondereffekten im Energiegeschäft im Vergleich zum Vorquartal mit rund 100 Millionen Euro belasten. Die Gesamtverkaufsmenge an Kohlenwasserstoffen sank auf 225.000 von 242.000 Barrel Öläquivalent pro Tag, obwohl die Produktion leicht auf 294.000 von 291.000 Barrel stieg. Der realisierte Rohölpreis fiel auf 93,60 von 97,80 Dollar je Barrel, während der Erdgaspreis auf 49,20 von 37,80 Euro je Megawattstunde (MWh) kletterte. Zudem dürften Sondersteuern auf Übergewinne in Österreich und Rumänien den unbereinigten Nettogewinn der OMV mit 150 bis 200 Millionen Euro schmälern. Das bereinigte operative Ergebnis bleibt davon unberührt, der Cashflow wird größtenteils erst 2027 belastet. Deutlich besser entwickelte sich das Raffineriegeschäft. Die europäische Referenzmarge sprang auf 37,50 von 20,33 Dollar je Barrel, die Auslastung stieg auf 92 von 90 Prozent. Der Konzern rechnet daher mit einem höheren Beitrag seiner Beteiligungen am staatlichen Ölkonzern Adnoc(ADNOC.UL) aus Abu Dhabi, was voraussichtlich schwächere Margen im Endkunden- und Gewerbegeschäft abfedert. Im Chemiegeschäft erwartet OMV dagegen einen deutlichen Ergebnisrückgang gegenüber dem zweiten Quartal. Ausschlaggebend sei ein erheblich schwächeres Marktumfeld für die Kunststoff-Beteiligung Borouge International in allen Regionen. Die Referenzmargen für Ethylen und Propylen in Europa gingen zurück, auch wenn die Auslastung der Steamcracker auf 82 von 77 Prozent stieg. Eine Borouge-Dividende von rund 460 Millionen Euro stützte dagegen den operativen Cashflow. Die Ergebnisse für das dritte Quartal will OMV am 29. Oktober vorlegen.

item.title: Global watchdog urges authorities to close gaps in emergency funding for failing banks
item.description: The Financial Stability Board, the global body that monitors risks to the financial system, urged authorities on Friday to strengthen emergency funding arrangements for failing banks after finding major gaps in countries' ability to provide liquidity during a crisis.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Financial Stability Board, the global body that monitors risks to the financial system, urged authorities on Friday to strengthen emergency funding arrangements for failing banks after finding major gaps in countries' ability to provide liquidity during a crisis. In a peer review of progress against its standards for resolving banks without resorting to taxpayer-funded bailouts, the FSB found fewer than half of jurisdictions had funding arrangements that were clearly defined, large enough and capable of being deployed quickly The review forms part of work launched after 2023 banking turmoil, including the collapse of Credit Suisse. Credit Suisse was [USN:L8N45F0DE TEXT:"taken over by UBS "] (UBSG.S) in a Swiss government-engineered rescue after suffering severe liquidity stress. The deal was supported by emergency liquidity facilities, a government liquidity backstop and the writedown of Additional Tier 1 bonds Recent bank failures had demonstrated how quickly lenders could come under acute liquidity stress, the FSB said It recommended that authorities identify in advance what temporary public funding could be made available during a bank failure, establish a clear legal basis for providing support and ensure they have powers to recover any losses, among other recommendations "Having a credible public sector backstop funding mechanism is essential," said Soledad Núñez, deputy governor of the Bank of Spain and chair of the peer review.

item.title: Ukraine fortifies its filling stations against Russian attacks
item.description: Sand-filled blast barriers and concrete shelters are multiplying at filling stations in Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash
item.content:encoded: Sand-filled blast barriers and concrete shelters are multiplying at filling stations in Ukraine in a push by retailers to fortify their networks as Russia attacks fuel infrastructure in major cities. Russia has struck petrol stations in frontline areas since the beginning of the full-scale war in 2022, but in recent months it has broadened its air campaign to target fuel retailers in Kyiv, Dnipro and Kharkiv. A senior executive at state-owned Ukrnafta, Ukraine's largest oil company, said it was taking steps to protect its facilities and the strikes would not cause shortages this winter despite an expected increase in demand of 10-15%. Even when petrol stations are hit, operations are sometimes restored within days, said Lesya Zharska, director of Ukrnafta's station network. "We will protect the facilities. We will restore the facilities. We are ready for the winter," she said in an interview at an Ukrnafta station on the outskirts of Kyiv. on the other side of the road, workers were rebuilding a station destroyed in a recent attack. In recent weeks, at least six Ukrnafta filling stations have been hit in Kyiv. In total, Russia has destroyed more than 300 stations in the last six months, Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said. Moscow says it does not deliberately target Ukraine's civilian infrastructure but it has stepped up attacks on populated areas as its forces struggle to advance on the ground. Meanwhile, Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries have caused fuel shortages in Russia, which has introduced an export ban. MITIGATING RISKS To mitigate the risks in population centres such as Kyiv, where it has three dozen of its 660 stations, Ukrnafta has put up blast barriers made of wire-mesh cubes - or gabions - filled with sand. The aim is to instal them in other cities soon. "When there is a yellow or red air alarm, we stop operations and ask customers to leave, and staff head to shelters," Zharska said. Russia is widely expected to intensify strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure once again as temperatures drop in winter. Ukrnafta has already equipped stations across its network with back-up diesel generators and contracted sufficient fuel imports to prevent supply gaps, Zharska said, adding: "We will carry out our work."

item.title: Central banks face test. Will they be good cops or bond villains?
item.description: A standoff between central banks and their cash-strapped governments may well be looming as an intensifying bond market crunch reopens questions about the political independence of the banks well beyond their interest-rate policy.
item.dc:creator: Mike Dolan
item.content:encoded: A standoff between central banks and their cash-strapped governments may well be looming as an intensifying [USN:L6N45U0LN TEXT:"bond market crunch"] reopens questions about the political independence of the banks well beyond their interest-rate policy. Central banks currently appear reluctant to rebuild holdings of sovereign debt, yet those holdings played a significant role in the swelling public borrowing over the past decade. Moving forward, that means either an improbable fiscal tightening will need to emerge or political knives will be sharpened. Numerous elections in the US, France, Italy and Spain over the coming year mean significant spending cuts are unlikely to be on the agenda. If bond markets continue to tighten — as we've seen in recent weeks — political pressure on central banks to steady the ship will rise even further. Seeing the problem coming like a slow-motion car crash, central banks are trying to nuance their position. On one hand, a post-pandemic consensus has built around further "normalization" of their bond-packed balance sheets. This includes a retrospective disdain for using bond accumulation as a monetary policy tool. On the other hand, policymakers want to keep all options open for temporary fixes in the event of market malfunctioning or another left-field shock. Bank for International Settlements (BIS) boss Pablo Hernandez de Cos this week laid out some principles for using emergency tools if conditions get rough, using the example of the Bank of England's (BoE) limited and brief support for stressed British gilts during the budget blow-up in 2022. "A key challenge is to bolster market confidence without overstimulating the economy in the longer term," he said of such emergency tools. "Central banks should try to better distinguish programmes for market functioning from those for monetary stimulus." But the problem with a middle-ground, [USN:L6N45T16X TEXT:"only-in-emergencies"] approach is that sometimes debt markets can get squeezed even when there isn't an acute crisis. Just look at the current global bond selloff. Markets are not necessarily malfunctioning, and despite the clear energy hit from the Iran war , there's no global shock on the scale of COVID-19 or the 2008 banking crash to justify a red alert. Yet markets continue to inflict maximum pain on government debt-service bills. Should this continue, alongside a relatively hot AI-infused economy and above-target inflation rates, monetary policymakers could find themselves in a very tough spot. If central banks do step in, the lines between "backstops," monetary policy and direct government support could become blurred, and central bankers could once again find themselves criticised for enabling rising government debt loads. Yet governments across the developed world may expect them to do just that if sovereign bond yields keep increasing. Rising debt-service bills are coming at a time when ageing demographics in most Group of Seven (G7) economies have already been heaping pressure on pension and healthcare systems, while defence spending is set to spiral higher amid increasingly fraught geopolitics. Pointing to forecasts that global government debt will exceed annual global GDP by 2030, [USN:L1N45S0Z3 TEXT:"International Monetary Fund head Kristalina Georgieva"] this week warned rich governments to deliver credible fiscal-consolidation plans urgently and not fall back on central banks to bail them out. "I would call this 'monetary cowboys', running to the rescue of the fiscal agents, and my message is: please don't." HOW DID WE GET HERE? For context, we need to rewind a bit. Of the multiple reasons cited for the intense government bond market selloff in recent months, a big question revolves around the gaping hole left in debt markets by the gradual withdrawal of G7 central banks from the swelling debt piles they facilitated following 2008. The selloff has pushed long-term US sovereign borrowing costs to their highest in almost a quarter of a century. Perhaps the best way to understand how artificially cheap borrowing distorted the picture is to examine how quickly governments accumulated debt when their central banks were buying bonds and effectively underwriting large chunks of it. The Washington-based Institute of International Finance recently estimated that even though average government borrowing costs across the G7 are back at mid-2008 levels, annual interest expenses are 85% higher because G7 government debts have almost trebled to more than $60 trillion in the interim. Advanced economies collectively are now paying over $3.3 trillion to service bonds alone, it said, which is more than their estimated spending on either AI, defence or clean energy. But coinciding with, and aggravating, the recent surge in government debt costs has been the steady pruning of central bank balance sheets over the past four years. The aggregate G7 central bank balance sheet peaked at over $30 trillion of bonds in early 2022 and has been cut by about a third since then.Along with the sharp rise in central bank policy rates to choke off inflation, that one-third reduction has coincided with a 40% drop in long-term G7 government bond indexes and a four-percentage-point spike in their implied borrowing rate. Have central banks exited too much or too quickly, and should they pause that withdrawal until they rethink it? BALANCE SHEET PHILOSOPHY Opinion on the wisdom of so-called quantitative easing (QE) — massive central-bank bond-buying programs — has done an almost 180-degree turn since the inflation spikes and debt explosions of the pandemic and its aftermath. For many, the banking crash of 2008 and 2020's COVID-19 lockdowns justified extraordinary one-off balance sheet reactions from the Federal Reserve and others. But many also now criticize the continuous use of bond buying as an ongoing monetary tool, arguing that it underwrote the massive expansion of government debt over the past 20 years. Much of the central bank world now feels the experiment may have been misguided at best, both because it tiptoed into quasi-fiscal territory and because of a variety of market distortions and inequality questions that arose from what was essentially direct support for wealthier asset owners. New Fed Chair and long-time balance-sheet-expansion sceptic [USN:S8N40E0AX TEXT:"Kevin Warsh "]claims the whole 18-year QE episode "borders on fiscal policy." He has already set up one of his Fed reform task forces to look at ways to reduce the balance sheet holdings further. On the other side of the pond, the [USN:L8N4590WV TEXT:"BoE"] is still actively selling gilts, albeit with recent plans to concentrate sales in short-dated paper. And the European Central Bank is still actively running down its balance sheet, which amounts to more than 40% of euro zone GDP, even as the region faces echoes of the 2011-12 euro debt crisis in French bond markets. A change of [USN:L6N45R0YE TEXT:"ECB leadership"] is also on the horizon, and the leading candidates don't appear to have an appetite for a return to the 2010s and the firefighting activism of former chief Mario Draghi. TWITCHIER TREASURIES There is also the question of who is holding government debt. The reduction of G7 central bank bond holdings has coincided with reduced pension-fund demand for long-dated government debt as defined-benefit schemes dwindle and pension savers retire. Those gaps left by long-term investors keen on safety and steady coupons have increasingly been filled by more speculative, short-term players such as hedge funds, who are much more sensitive to big price shifts, vulnerable to short-term interest rate changes and prone to herding in volatile conditions. Hedge fund activity in sovereign bond markets has been the focus of regulators for years. While everyone welcomes the demand and liquidity they provide, there is now growing concern about the flipside of that if this "fast money" base gets twitchy. Some efforts have been made to reduce [USN:L6N45R0WM TEXT:"excessive leverage"] in government bond markets, but no matter how that pans out, the scale of [USN:L6N44U0ZU TEXT:"hedge fund activity"] in these markets, and by extension the exposure of the banks and trading houses that provide them with leverage, makes for a more skittish environment. "These buyers are more inclined to sell bonds in response to higher short-term interest rates — funding leg sensitivity — and charge a higher price for the risk of further upward moves," wrote Carlyle strategist Jason Thomas. "When coupled with the growth in the outstanding volume of debt, this new class of investors has left bond markets more fragile and sensitized to front-end repricing." This sensitivity helps to explain the recent disturbance in Treasury markets, which seems to have been driven largely by the Fed changing course on short-term rates. SMBC Nikko's rates strategist Joseph Abate cites Fed studies trying to quantify that sensitivity. Fed economist Phillip Monin estimates that hedge fund demand for [USN:L1N45E0NO TEXT:"cash-futures arbitrage plays "]has increased fourfold since 2020 and is now 3.5% of outstanding Treasury supply. Another Fed study last month by Daniel Beltran and Canlin Li found that the market's sensitivity to new supply had doubled over the past decade, with every 1% increase in new debt, some $300 billion or more, increasing 5-year yields by 8 basis points. Regulators, governments and central banks are watching this closely. But any planned tightening of rules could well have adverse effects at a politically risky moment. While the answer, in theory, may be reducing the supply of government debt, in practice, that is very unlikely to occur. The alternative solution lands back in the lap of now more hesitant central banks — kicking and screaming perhaps. (The opinions expressed here are those of Mike Dolan , a columnist for Reuters.) item.title: Cheap coal and expensive gas set stage for year-end coal export surge
item.description: Global exports of thermal coal are currently on track to register a second consecutive annual contraction. But thanks to thermal coal's widest price discount to LNG in four years, coal shipments look set for a late-year resurgence.
item.dc:creator: Gavin Maguire
item.content:encoded: Global exports of thermal coal are currently on track to register a second consecutive annual contraction. But thanks to thermal coal's widest price discount to LNG in four years, coal shipments look set for a late-year resurgence. Benchmark Australian thermal coal export prices are currently around 80% cheaper than liquefied natural gas for delivery in Asia, which cements coal's place as the most affordable power generation fuel in the region. The fourth quarter of the year is also the traditional high point for coal demand in Asia, which is when utilities replenish stocks ahead of the winter heating period. That combination of a growing price advantage over alternate fuels just as the peak demand period kicks in has the potential to propel coal export volumes sharply higher over the final weeks of the year. For climate trackers hoping to see a permanent decline in coal use, any late-year renaissance in coal flows may be a disappointment. But for utilities across the world's most populous region, the economics of generation may trump climate concerns over the near term, and ensure coal retains its central role in power production mixes across Asia. WIDE SPREAD Australian export prices of thermal coal from Newcastle are currently trading around $143 per metric ton, or the equivalent of around $5.40 per million British thermal units (MMBtu), according to LSEG. That compares to the latest quotes for LNG delivered to Asia of around $25.00 per MMBtu, and so means that high-quality thermal coal is roughly $20 per MMBtu cheaper than LNG in key Asian power markets. With thermal coal prices from Indonesia — the world's largest thermal coal exporter — routinely at least $1 per MMBtu cheaper than Australian coal, power generators across Asia have a strong economic incentive to opt for coal over LNG for the upcoming winter heating season. PEAK BURN Power fuel importers are already into the fuel restocking cycle in preparation for a pick-up in heating demand across major coal-consuming markets such as China, Japan and South Korea. Those three countries between them imported around 122 million metric tons of coal during the July-through-September quarter, data from commodities intelligence firm Kpler shows, which is when power demand for cooling peaks in those countries. However, those same countries imported an average of 143 million tons of thermal coal during the last quarter of the year in 2024 and 2025, which is when heating demand peaks. That means that the combined coal imports of China, Japan and South Korea alone could jump by around 20 million tons during the last quarter of the year compared to the previous quarter. For major coal exporters such as Indonesia and Australia, those import trends tend to mean that the final months of the year are usually the busiest in terms of ensuring exported supplies meet those elevated demand levels. Export data for Indonesia show that average shipment volumes during the October-to-December quarter averaged around 137 million tons for the 2023 to 2025 period, and were the highest for any quarter for those years. During the third quarter of 2026, Indonesia shipped out just under 107 million tons, which was the lowest tally for that quarter since 2021. Australia also tends to see export volumes reach their peak during the final quarter, and averaged around 55 million tons for the October-to-December period from 2023 through 2025. During the third quarter this year, Australia's export tally was 52 million tons. UPTURN If utilities across East Asia ramp up their coal import orders in line with previous years for the final quarter of 2026, Indonesia and Australia will both see a significant rise in purchase orders. Indeed, combined fourth-quarter volumes out of Indonesia and Australia averaged around 192.5 million tons from 2023 through 2025, Kpler data shows. Total exports from those countries were around 159 million tons during the July-to-September quarter of 2026, and so could see a nearly 30-million-ton climb during the final quarter of 2026 if previous trends are repeated. If that seasonal lift materialises, it would mark a notable turnaround for a fuel whose long-term outlook is widely viewed as being in decline. Yet coal's enduring advantage is that it competes on price rather than policy. With LNG prices elevated and power demand entering its strongest seasonal phase, utilities across Asia may conclude that the cheapest source of electricity is also the hardest fuel to replace. For all the momentum behind the energy transition, this winter's trade flows could serve as a reminder that cost still shapes fuel choices more than climate ambitions across much of the region. item.title: New Zealand censor says it would be powerless to block livestreamed US execution
item.description: New Zealand's national censor said on Friday it would be unable to block the planned livestreamed execution of a former Army major in the United States, as rights groups pressed governments to protest the decision with Washington.
item.dc:creator: Alasdair Pal
item.content:encoded: New Zealand's national censor said on Friday it would be unable to block the planned livestreamed execution of a former Army major in the United States, as rights groups pressed governments to protest the decision with Washington. Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009. The [USN:L1N45U124 TEXT:"Pentagon said on Thursday"] Hasan's December 3 execution by firing squad would be livestreamed, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution. The decision is likely to draw scrutiny from governments around the world amid mounting efforts to protect young people in particular from harmful internet content. One of the first countries to react was New Zealand, where censorship authorities highlighted difficulties in restricting access to such material. "The Classification Office cannot classify a livestream event as it is taking place, and we, nor any other body, has the authority to block access to a livestream event," a spokesperson for New Zealand's Classification Office said in a statement. "The threshold for banning content under New Zealand law is high and requires that we balance freedom of expression with the likelihood of harm," New Zealand Chief Censor Caroline Flora said. "Distressing as content may be, it is not always unlawful." The news has additional resonance in New Zealand, where a gunman killed 51 people at two mosques in 2019, livestreaming his crimes on Facebook. The country has since been at the forefront of combating violent content online, with then-Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern [USN:L1N2MV00L TEXT:"launching a global campaign"] on the issue months after the attack. US Defense SecretaryPete Hegseth said the execution by firing squad was a "no-brainer", adding that people need to understand there are "serious consequences for these types of things." Under US military law, a US president must approve an execution. President Donald Trump did so on Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon said on Monday. The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon. Public executions have become exceedingly rare worldwide. Among countries known to conduct them in recent years are Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan. The decision was criticised by rights groups, with Amnesty International Australia urging Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to press the US to reverse its decision. "The suggestion that an execution by firing squad should be livestreamed for public viewing is an appalling disregard for human dignity," said Kyinzom Dhongdue, a campaign manager at the rights group. "Turning a state-sanctioned killing into a public spectacle only compounds the cruelty of the death penalty." Spokespeople for the foreign ministries of Australia and New Zealand did not respond to requests for comment.

item.content:encoded: Indonesia is forging ahead with a plan to shift ownership of a majority stake in the operator of a $7.3 billion China-funded bullet train, despite missing the target date last month, a senior official said on Friday. The government initially planned to transfer the 60% stake in the "Whoosh" bullet train operator from a consortium of state companies to government agencies on [USN:L4N4500HZ TEXT:"September 15"], but an [USN:L1N45606D TEXT:"abrupt change"] in the finance ministry leadership delayed that Several ministries and sovereign wealth fund Danantara were drafting a presidential decree for the process, which would include a transfer of liabilities, finance ministry official Evita Manthovani said on Friday, without giving a timeline Chinese state companies hold the remaining 40% stake The operator has been struggling to repay a bank loan used to fund the project as passenger numbers have not reached the intended level The government's decision on how to handle debt repayments to China must also take into account fiscal sustainability, Manthovani told a press conference The bullet train, covering 142 km (88 miles) between Jakarta and Bandung, started operations in 2023, after facing problems including delays and cost overruns

item.title: LeBron James scores 10 points in 76ers preseason debut
item.description: LeBron James showcased his passing ability in his first action wearing a Philadelphia uniform, taking just one official shot but compiling five assists on Thursday in his first preseason game with the 76ers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: LeBron James showcased his passing ability in his first action wearing a Philadelphia uniform, taking just one official shot but compiling five assists on Thursday in his first preseason game with the 76ers. James wound up with 10 points, thanks to 8-for-8 shooting from the foul line, as the Sixers lost 114-108 to the Brooklyn Nets in New York. The 41-year-old star sat out the second half. After James didn't appear in Philadelphia's preseason opener on Monday against the NBA champion New York Knicks, he played Thursday to give the 76ers a glimpse at their revamped starting lineup. James and fellow newcomer Jaylen Brown teamed with Philadelphia holdovers Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe and Joel Embiid. "Obviously, I was wearing a new uniform, but the game is the game, and the game is needed to be played on the floor," James said. "And I was happy to be able to log some minutes with the guys that we've been going at each other in practice for the last two weeks, a week and a half, or whatever the case may be." In the first quarter, James logged four points, all on free throws, and five assists. His lone basket came near the midpoint of the second period, when he sank a layup to put Philadelphia on top 40-39. James signed a two-year, $8 million deal with a player option to join the 76ers as a free agent in July. In 60 games for the Lakers last season, James averaged 20.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 7.2 assists, down from his career norms of 26.8, 7.5 and 7.4, respectively. The 22-time All-Star is the NBA's all-time leader in games played (1,622) and points (43,440). He won championship rings with the Miami Heat (2011-12 and 2012-13), the Cleveland Cavaliers (2015-16) and the Los Angeles Lakers (2019-20). --Field Level Media

item.title: El Niño has strengthened to strongest on record, Japan weather agency says
item.description: The El Niño phenomenon has strengthened to its strongest on record since September, Japan's weather bureau said on Friday, adding that there was a 100% chance the conditions will continue into the Northern hemisphere winter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The El Niño phenomenon has strengthened to its strongest on record since September, Japan's weather bureau said on Friday, adding that there was a 100% chance the conditions will continue into the Northern hemisphere winter. The sea surface temperature anomaly in the El Niño monitoring region was plus 4.0 degrees Celsius (7.2 degrees Fahrenheit) in September, the highest since records began in 1949, the Japan Meteorological Agency said.

item.title: Rookie's shootout goal caps Golden Knights' rally against Maple Leafs
item.description: Trevor Connelly scored on a backhand shot in the fifth round of a shootout as the Vegas Golden Knights rallied from an early three-goal deficit to defeat the Toronto Maple Leafs 4-3 on Thursday in Las Vegas.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Trevor Connelly scored on a backhand shot in the fifth round of a shootout as the Vegas Golden Knights rallied from an early three-goal deficit to defeat the Toronto Maple Leafs 4-3 on Thursday in Las Vegas. It was the first career shootout try for Connelly, a 20-year-old rookie. He faked a forehand shot and then pulled the puck back and wrapped the backhand shot around the left pad of Sergei Bobrovsky for the game-winner. Toronto's John Tavares then had a chance to force a sixth round in the shootout, but Adin Hill made a pad save on his wrist shot. The only other skaters who converted their shootout opportunities were Vegas' Braeden Bowman and Toronto's Kirill Marchenko, both in the first round. Jack Eichel scored on a penalty shot and also had an assist and Mark Stone and Brett Howden also scored in regulation for Vegas, which won its third straight game. Hill made 21 saves. Jack Roslovic, Easton Cowan and Nick Paul scored goals for Toronto, which was opening a three-game western road trip. Bobrovsky finished with a season-high 40 saves while falling to 0-2-1. Toronto jumped out to a 3-0 lead in the first 8:37 of the game. Roslovic, making his 600th career NHL appearance, started the scoring just 34 seconds into the contest when he squeaked a backhand shot from the right side of the crease over Hill's left pad and just inside the right post. It was his second goal of the season and his 300th career point. Cowan made it 2-0 with a breakaway goal, taking a stretch pass from Chris Tanev and beating Hill with a wrist shot on his blocker side at 3:20. Paul extended the lead to 3-0 when he deflected a one-timer by Darren Raddysh over Hill's left shoulder for his first goal with the Maple Leafs. Stone got Vegas on the scoreboard near the end of the opening period with his third goal, a slap shot from the top of the right circle off an Eichel drop pass. The Golden Knights dominated the second period, outshooting Toronto 21-8 while scoring twice to tie it 3-3. Howden got the first goal when Mitch Marner's crossing pass from the right circle deflected into the net off his skate at 1:12. Eichel, awarded a penalty shot when he was tripped driving the net by Morgan Rielly at 3:58, fired a wrist shot under Bobrovsky's glove from the slot for his third goal. It was his second successful penalty shot in four career tries. --Field Level Media

item.title: US 10-year Treasury yield risks hitting 6% for first time since 2000, Pimco's Ivascyn tells FT
item.description: The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield could rise to 6% for the first time since 2000 as high oil prices fuel inflation concerns and worries over the country's growing public debt, Dan Ivascyn, Chief Investment Officer at bond fund manager Pimco, told the Financial Times.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield could rise to 6% for the first time since 2000 as high oil prices fuel inflation concerns and worries over the country's growing public debt, Dan Ivascyn, Chief Investment Officer at bond fund manager Pimco, told the Financial Times. US Treasury yields are a yardstick for global borrowing costs and asset prices. The 10-year yield has [USN:L6N45T06X TEXT:"risen"] almost 120 basis points this year and is trading slightly below the 5.34% level it hit last week, its highest since 2002. A sharp rise from the current level of 5.29% was "feasible" in the near term, Ivascyn told FT on Friday, citing factors such as hedge funds unwinding their losing bond positions. "It is certainly possible, even from a short-term trading perspective, given that some of the activity we've seen in the last couple of weeks is tied to some negative technicals, some stop-out activity from the platform hedge funds and other levered investors. You can certainly get there," he said. If Treasury yields rose further, it could weigh on riskier assets such as stocks and corporate bonds, he said, adding that a move to 5.5% or higher would likely lead to "some decent weakness in risk markets, both credit and equity". Global bonds have come under heavy selling pressure this year as soaring energy costs fan inflation and the AI boom lifts economic growth, leaving investors positioning for an era where interest rates stay higher for longer. Bond yields, which rise when prices fall, have consequently soared globally, with the US 10-year Treasury yield posting its [USN:L1N45N05N TEXT:"biggest quarterly rise"] this century for the three months ending in September.

item.title: L'ouragan Isaias se renforce à l'approche des côtes américaines
item.description: L'ouragan Isaias s'est renforcé jeudi alors qu'il se dirigeait la côte des Etats-Unis dans le Golfe du Mexique, provoquant des évacuations et la déclaration de l'état d'urgence en Floride et dans l'Alabama alors que les météorologues ont mis en garde contre de dangereuses ondes de tempêtes, des tornades et des inondations.
item.dc:creator: Brad Brooks
item.content:encoded: L'ouragan Isaias s'est renforcé jeudi alors qu'il se dirigeait la côte des Etats-Unis dans le Golfe du Mexique, provoquant des évacuations et la déclaration de l'état d'urgence en Floride et dans l'Alabama alors que les météorologues ont mis en garde contre de dangereuses ondes de tempêtes, des tornades et des inondations. Le premier ouragan de la saison, dont les vents atteignaient tôt jeudi 140 kilomètres/heure (km/h), devrait presque atteindre la catégorie 3 vendredi, avec des vents atteignant les 175 km/h. Isaias devrait atteindre la côte nord du Golfe du Mexique vendredi soir ou samedi matin. "Nous nous attendons à ce qu'Isaias soit un ouragan dangereux lorsqu'il touchera terre", a dit jeudi le directeur du Centre national des ouragans (NHC) des Etats-Unis, Michael Brennan. "Il faut aujourd'hui se préparer." Les compagnies pétrolières ont évacué leurs installations offshores du Golfe du Mexique et arrêté leurs opérations. Le NHC a émis des alertes ouragan dans les zones côtières du Mississippi, en Alabama et en Floride. Des alertes pour une tempête tropicale et des ondes de tempêtes ont également été émises dans le sud-est de la Louisiane. Des évacuations ont été ordonnées en Floride où l'état d'urgence a été déclaré dans 25 comtés plus tôt dans la semaine. Trois aéroports du comté d'Okaloosa devraient fermer jeudi soir. L'état d'urgence a été déclaré dans 40 comtés de l'Alabama, où des évacuations ont également été ordonnées. Selon les météorologues, l'onde de tempête pourrait atteindre de 1,5 à 2,1 mètres dans les zones les plus touchées, tandis que de 8 à 18 cm de précipitations sont attendus. Jeudi après-midi, l'ouragan se trouvait à près de 570 kilomètres au sud de l'embouchure du Mississippi et se déplaçait vers l'est-nord-est à une vitesse de 17km/h, a indiqué le NHC.

item.title: POINT MARCHÉS Wall Street en ordre dispersé avec la hausse des prix du pétrole
item.description: La Bourse de New York a fini en ordre dispersé jeudi, seul le Dow Jones marquant une petite hausse, alors que les prix du pétrole ont bondi en raison d'attaques autour du détroit d'Ormuz et d'une baisse de la production américaine, alimentant les craintes sur l'inflation et la hausse des taux d'intérêt.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Culp, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: La Bourse de New York a fini en ordre dispersé jeudi, seul le Dow Jones marquant une petite hausse, alors que les prix du pétrole ont bondi en raison d'attaques autour du détroit d'Ormuz et d'une baisse de la production américaine, alimentant les craintes sur l'inflation et la hausse des taux d'intérêt. L'indice Dow Jones (.DJI) a gagné 0,10%, ou 51,77 points, à 51.231,64 points. Le S&P-500 (.SPX) , plus large, a perdu 36,41 points, soit 0,47%, à 7.765,36 points. Le Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) a reculé de son côté de 345,35 points (1,25%) à 27.193,34 points. Deux jours après avoir atteint un record de clôture, le Nasdaq a subi la plus forte perte, plombé par le repli de 3,4% du secteur des semiconducteurs après que le Financial Times a rapporté que les revenus annualisés d'OpenAI ont été inférieurs de 20 milliards de dollars au montant signalé au préalable. Le marché connaît "une sortie de route" dans la perspective de la saison des résultats trimestriels et avec "le conflit en Iran qui fait monter les prix du pétrole", a commenté Terry Sandven, stratégiste en chef chez US Bank Wealth Management, à Minneapolis dans le Minnesota. Une série d'attaques contre des pétroliers dans le détroit d'Ormuz et une baisse de production aux Etats-Unis causée par des ouragans ont contribué à une nouvelle flambée des prix du brut, le baril WTI prenant 3,6% et le Brent 4,1%. L'approvisionnement amoindri en pétrole depuis le début de la guerre en Iran en février dernier a fait grimper les prix du brut de plus de 60% cette année, alimentant les pressions inflationnistes et laissant entrevoir un resserrement monétaire. C'est dans ce contexte que la Réserve fédérale (Fed) a opéré en septembre sa première hausse des taux depuis juillet 2023. Si les marchés financiers s'attendent à ce que la banque centrale américaine laisse ses taux inchangés en octobre, ils misent à environ 69% sur l'hypothèse d'un relèvement des taux lors de la réunion de décembre, d'après FedWatch de CME. Les rendements des bons du Trésor américain ont progressé jeudi, atteignant des niveaux proches de leurs records, tandis que les obligations à courte échéance ont bondi. Parmi les secteurs majeurs du S&P-500, l'énergie (.SPNY) a connu la plus forte hausse du jour. Côté valeurs, à noter, PepsiCo (PEP.O) a pris 3,7% après avoir annoncé une réduction supplémentaire de ses coûts et revu à la baisse sa prévision de bénéfice annuel. Starbucks (SBUX.O) a cédé 0,4% à la suite d'informations de presse selon lesquelles le groupe envisage de racheter Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG.N) , dont le titre a bondi de 6,2%. Palantir (PLTR.O) a fini en hausse de 2,4% après que Goldman Sachs a revu sa recommandation à "acheter" contre "neutre".
