POLANSKI FACES DOWN CRITICS It was an early test for Burnham, whose predecessor, Starmer, stood down [USN:L8N44T0YP TEXT:"as a lawmaker in September"] after being ousted as [USN:L1N43M05W TEXT:"prime minister"] in July. Under Starmer, Labour had also ceded ground to t[USN:L8N4171WM TEXT:"he Green Party"], which made record gains in London in May's local elections with its widening appeal among younger, left-leaning voters in the capital and other urban areas. The Greens have fallen back in opinion polls since, after Burnham made policy pitches that boosted Labour's standing among voters to the left, including a [USN:L8N45007X TEXT:"tougher line on Israel"] and a more ambitious approach to [USN:L1N45M0A5 TEXT:"relations with the European Union"]. Polanski, who is Jewish, was questioned repeatedly after the by-election over the conference vote on Zionism and the Green leader seemed again to distance himself from it, saying only that he believed displacement of Palestinian people and "ongoing genocide" were racist. For now, he said, the Green Party should take their fight to Burnham's Labour and focus on whether the governing party's budget on October 28 delivers. "So many people told me on the doorstep that they want to give Andy Burnham a chance," Polanski told broadcasters. "Well, he's got a chance now. Let's see what he does with it."

item.title: Modi wants India to power the AI age. Residents are pushing back
item.description: The view from Indian engineer Tushar Shetty's Mumbai apartment captures a tension playing out around the world as the artificial intelligence boom fuels an unprecedented data-centre building spree.
item.dc:creator: Vibhuti Sharma, Munsif Vengattil, Aditya Kalra
item.content:encoded: The view from Indian engineer Tushar Shetty's Mumbai apartment captures a tension playing out around the world as the artificial intelligence boom fuels an unprecedented data-centre building spree. What was once a stretch of lush greenery outside his 21st-floor window is now a scar of red earth where trees were felled to make way for an Amazon facility that forms part of the tech giant's planned $21 billion investment in AI infrastructure in India by 2030. "I would not have bought the house if I had known," said the 46-year-old, lamenting a purchase made just five months ago. From the suburbs of Virginia to the outskirts of Amsterdam and Dublin, residents have increasingly rebelled against the spread of AI data centres, complaining of noise, surging electricity consumption, water stress and industrialisation of residential neighbourhoods. Workers and excavators operate at the site of an Amazon data centre in Thane, India, September 22, 2026. REUTERS/Francis Mascarenhas That resistance is gaining ground in India, where Amazon, Google and Microsoft are pouring billions into facilities that advance Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ambition to host "the whole world's data", stretching from Maharashtra in the west to Andhra Pradesh in the south. Unable for now to match the frontier models emerging from the US and China, India is pursuing a different path, betting that dominance in the physical backbone of artificial intelligence may prove just as valuable. The strategy sits at the heart of Modi's investment pitch as the world's back office loses its shine, even as the ambition collides with concerns over scarce resources and communities living alongside the infrastructure powering the digital economy. India holds 4% of the world's freshwater for 18% of its people, and data centres are clustering in cities already short of it. S&P Global estimates 60% to 80% of Indian data centres could face high water stress this decade. In 2025, data centres used about 150 billion litres of water, a figure projected to more than double by 2030, according to research firm Mordor Intelligence. The Amazon project near Mumbai is emerging as one of India's most prominent flashpoints. Reuters interviews with more than two dozen residents and a review of official correspondence show growing concerns it will strain local power and water supplies and generate noise harmful to health, particularly for children and the elderly. Amazon and local authorities have strongly defended the project, saying it will not burden public utilities because water and power will come from dedicated sources. The dispute has nevertheless sparked street protests and drawn opposition politicians into the fight. Modi's government has also mounted a public defence, promoting data centres online as "the invisible engines powering India's digital life" and arguing modern technologies use water and electricity more efficiently. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the Prime Minister's Office and Maharashtra's chief minister's office did not respond to requests for comment. On September 8, hundreds of residents, including elderly people, gathered beside the site holding placards reading "Data centres are energy vampires". They want the project moved elsewhere. Residentes portan pancartas durante una protesta contra el centro de datos que Amazon planea construir en Thane, en las afueras de Bombay, India, el 8 de septiembre de 2026. Fotografía tomada con un teléfono móvil. REUTERS/Vibhuti Sharma "If the data centre stops, we will stay ... If it goes ahead, we will move," said Vasudha Shetty, 62, who bought a flat near the 54-acre planned facility, but wants to prioritize a quiet retirement. AMAZON WEIGHS COMMUNITY OUTREACH More than 1,000 residents living near the site say the project was pushed through without meaningful consultation. In Virginia, home to the world's largest concentration of data centres, Amazon paused a 2024 proposal for three facilities amid concerns over noise and proximity to homes, saying it wanted more time for community engagement. Mumbai residents say they never got that chance. Internally, Amazon is not overly concerned because government officials have indicated the protests will pass, according to a person familiar with its planning. Still, the company is drawing up community outreach plans to address concerns over noise, water and power. "Building data centres comes at a cost. Amazon at a global level is prepared to work with community and limit any inconvenience," the person said. "For now there is no other option but to live with protests." Amazon told Reuters the data centre will use water-free cooling, a dedicated power supply separate from homes and noise-mitigation measures. It added that more saplings were planted than trees removed. Still, even some industry executives question whether data centres belong next to neighbourhoods. "I will never set up a data centre in a residential area," Sharad Agarwal, CEO of Sify Infinit Spaces, which runs 14 data centres, said at an industry event in September. "Centres need abundant, uninterrupted power and water ... and near homes they risk being starved of both in a shortage." Microsoft has also unveiled a four-year $20.5 billion investment plan for India, mostly earmarked for AI data centres. POLITICAL SNAGS In the southern state of Andhra Pradesh, environmentalists are opposing [USN:L4N4421ED TEXT:"Google's $15 billion data centre project"], citing risks to wildlife, water and power supplies and alleging that a temple's land was used without permission. Google and the state deny any wrongdoing. The backlash has also turned political. In September, Aaditya Thackeray, an opposition legislator, joined Mumbai protesters demanding the Amazon project be relocated, saying his party would move it if returned to power. Back in Mumbai, property broker Atul Jadhav said buyer concerns over views and property values may be hurting nearby resale prices. "We will come out on the roads and do whatever it takes to stop it," said Vidya Kadam, 68, who has lived in the area for 30 years.

item.title: Gold rises more than 1%, Fed outlook in focus
item.description: Gold rose more than 1% on Friday, helped by a softer US dollar and lower oil prices, while market players weighed lingering inflation concerns and the outlook for Federal Reserve interest rates.
item.dc:creator: Ashitha Shivaprasad
item.content:encoded: Gold rose more than 1% on Friday, helped by a softer US dollar and lower oil prices, while market players weighed lingering inflation concerns and the outlook for Federal Reserve interest rates. Spot gold rose 1.4% to $4,190.57 per ounce by 0630 GMT after hitting a two-month low on Wednesday. Prices headed for a weekly gain. US gold futures for December delivery gained 1.4% to $4,215.30. The dollar rally took a breather, making greenback-priced bullion more affordable for holders of other currencies. Oil prices fell as Middle East supply concerns eased somewhat after President [USN:L1N45U0PH TEXT:"Donald Trump"] said the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm congressional elections amid productive talks to end their war. "Possible tightening later on could keep gold at risk... Looking ahead, traders will watch upcoming economic data that could provide further monetary policy clues and influence sentiment ahead of the Federal Reserve’s October meeting," said Tony Sage, CEO of Critical Metals. "Softer numbers or guidance could push yields to the downside and support gold." Last month, the US central bank voted unanimously to [USN:L6N4570XW TEXT:"raise"] the policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point. St. Louis Fed President [USN:L6N45U16W TEXT:"Alberto Musalem"] said the US central bank will need to hike rates again to bring inflation back to its 2% target, although he declined to say what policymakers should do at their meeting later this month. Traders are pricing in a 17% chance of a rate hike in October and an 83% probability of an increase in December, according to CME's FedWatch tool. Gold is traditionally seen as a hedge against inflation, but higher interest rates diminish the appeal of the non-yielding asset. Among other metals, spot silver rose 1.5% to $60.22, platinum gained 2.7% to $1,677.80 and palladium climbed 3.3% to $1,159.70.

item.title: Stocks meander as AI spending worries, elevated yields weigh
item.description: Asian stocks were poised on Friday for a second straight weekly drop, as investors fretted about higher energy prices, bond market ructions and the huge sums needed to fund AI investment.
item.dc:creator: Ankur Banerjee
item.content:encoded: Asian stocks were poised on Friday for a second straight weekly drop, as investors fretted about higher energy prices, bond market ructions and the huge sums needed to fund AI investment. Brent crude futures dipped 1.2% to $103.05 per barrel after surging more than 4% in the previous session on concerns over the Middle East war that has fanned inflation worries and led to higher rates across the globe. In equities, MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) was set for a drop of nearly 1% on the week, although it was up 0.5% on the day in thin liquidity, as markets in South Korea and Taiwan shut for a holiday. Japan's Nikkei (.N225) dipped 0.25%, while European futures pointed to a higher open. Nasdaq futures rose 0.5% after tech stocks led Wall Street's main indexes lower overnight. Much of Friday's market focus was on OpenAI, after media gave an idea of the money the ChatGPT owner is making. Reuters reported that OpenAI told investors its annualised [USN:L6N45U1FJ TEXT:"September"] revenue was almost $50 billion, a drop from its earlier signal, although Bloomberg said the firm could reach or exceed $70 billion by year-end, helping to lift stocks. "The price action suggests investors are becoming more selective about where they want exposure and, importantly, what price they are prepared to pay for future growth," said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone. On Thursday, President Donald Trump said the US would [USN:L1N45U0PH TEXT:"not launch an attack"] on Iran before midterm elections in November, but traders stayed sceptical of progress towards ending the war. "The big question for markets is whether Trump sticks to his word if Iranian attacks intensify," said Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global. "Any indication that the White House is reconsidering military action could see oil prices spike sharply higher, particularly with tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz already under significant pressure." BOND BINGE FOR AI Investors were also weighing a massive round of fundraising that appeared to be planned, with SpaceX (SPCX.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) and Oracle (ORCL.N) all expected to raise billions to buy high-end AI chips. Australian data centre operator Firmus, backed by Nvidia (NVDA.O) , shelved its $5-billion [USN:L1N45U12T TEXT:"initial public offering"], citing market volatility and conditions, and said it would opt for a private fundraising round instead. A toxic mix of higher energy costs, expectations of central bank interest rate hikes and concerns over rising government debt have fuelled a months-long global bond selloff, pushing up borrowing costs. "With long-term yields back around multi-decade highs, investors no longer have the luxury of valuing AI growth in a low-cost-of-capital world," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. Higher sovereign yields, and now rising corporate issuance to fund AI infrastructure mean capital is becoming "both more expensive and more selective, which puts balance sheets and the quality of future earnings firmly in focus," Chanana said. FOCUS ON FRANCE France has been hit particularly hard as investors scrutinise its debt load, budget deficit and political outlook ahead of the 2027 presidential election. "The scale of the fiscal adjustment required in France is large but manageable," ANZ analysts said in a note, adding that the fractured political landscape poses a greater challenge, however. "Until a clearer political consensus forms, market pressures are likely to remain." US Treasury markets have been calmer as solid auctions this week helped the mood. The benchmark 10-year yield was steady at 5.226% but held close to the 24-year high of 5.364% hit on Wednesday. Among currencies, the dollar stood tall as the euro was set for a fifth straight week in the red at $1.123, straddling a 17-month low touched this week on French debt worries.

item.title: Firmus investor Maas falls after AI data-centre operator pulls blockbuster IPO plan
item.description: Shares of Australian construction services provider Maas Group fell nearly 11% on Friday after Nvidia -backed Firmus withdrew its $5 billion IPO, raising concerns over the value of Maas's 3.2% stake in the data-centre operator.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Shares of Australian construction services provider Maas Group (MGH.AX) fell nearly 11% on Friday after Nvidia (NVDA.O) -backed Firmus withdrew its $5 billion IPO, raising concerns over the value of Maas's 3.2% stake in the data-centre operator. The stock fell as much as 10.7% to a five-month low of A$4.43 after trading resumed from a halt pending an update on Firmus's IPO and Maas's contracts with the operator. Maas is both an investor in Firmus and a supplier through its JLE Group electrical infrastructure unit. Earlier in the day, Firmus [USN:L1N45U12T TEXT:"withdrew"] its listing application, citing market volatility and conditions that it said would not fairly reflect its business strength and long-term growth prospects. The company, which counts OpenAI as an anchor customer, said it would seek private funding and explore alternative public and private capital-raising options. FIRMUS CONTRACTS REMAIN IN PLACE JLE continues to deliver modular Power Cubes and related electrical scope for Firmus AI factory projects, with work orders worth about A$1.1 billion ($767.91 million) across fiscal 2026 and 2027, Maas said on Friday. Maas said it had received A$373 million in payments under the contracts and expects the work to be completed by the end of 2027. The stock [USN:L6N45U03Q TEXT:"slumped 22.4%"] on Thursday after a report that Firmus was reconsidering the deal's terms, wiping about A$517 million from Maas's market value. It has fallen more than 31% so far this week, on track for its worst week on record. Firmus had [USN:L1N45N0G2 TEXT:"planned"] to price its shares at A$11 each, valuing the company's equity at about A$30.6 billion, nearly triple its A$10.5 billion valuation from an August funding round. The withdrawn float, which would have been Australia's second-largest IPO on record, underscores investor caution toward highly valued AI infrastructure firms with aggressive expansion plans and significant funding requirements. ($1 = 1.4325 Australian dollars)

item.title: New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
item.description: US immigration agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday in his car with a child present in the Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitnesses.
item.dc:creator: Julia Harte, Kristina Cooke
item.content:encoded: US immigration agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday in his car with a child present in the Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitnesses. Federal immigration agents have shot at least 21 people since Republican President Donald Trump returned to office, [USN:L1N43J0KR TEXT:"7 fatally"], sparking protests across the US. Critics contend that Trump's push to [USN:L6N4510WH TEXT:"ramp up deportations"] has led to an [USN:L6N3YA11U TEXT:"increasing number of violent confrontations"], and accuse the administration of resisting accountability for the agents involved. Trump has said many migrants must be deported, blaming them, often in sweeping terms, for financial fraud and violent crimes. "Early reports indicate agents surrounded (the man) and a 5-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds," New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. "I have been on the phone with President Trump and (Homeland Security) Secretary Mullin, negotiating the release of the man ICE agents shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful," Mamdani said in a press conference late in the evening. He said he demanded from the Trump administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. "These actions are making the city less safe," Mamdani said. "This city wants ICE out. We want ICE out of our city, ICE out of our schools, ICE out of our hospitals, ICE out of our streets, ICE away from our kids." The mayor said the child in the car is physically unharmed. New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said NYPD has located the child with a family member after a wellness check. The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, said in a statement ICE officers were conducting a "targeted enforcement operation" in the Bronx, New York, to arrest a man from the Dominican Republic with a prior criminal conviction. The man identified as 28-year-old, had been arrested twice in New York City in 2023 and 2025, according to NYPD Commissioner Tisch. "During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured," DHS said, adding that ICE officers rendered immediate aid. "The individual is alive and at a local hospital." The shooting occurred at around 4 p.m. ET (2000 GMT), DHS said. Working at a restaurant near the shooting, Pedro Almarez said he heard shots fired and went outside to see several officers wearing ICE attire at the scene. "There were a lot of ICE officers, three or four cars," Almarez told Reuters by phone. He said NYPD officers arrived about 10 minutes later. He said the man was only removed from his car after an ambulance arrived. At the shooting scene, where police strung yellow crime-scene tape to cordon off a city block, a woman standing on a balcony overlooking the area told officers they were "taking our children," according to a Reuters witness.

item.title: Nvidia-backed Firmus scraps $5 billion Australian IPO as investors step up AI scrutiny
item.description: Australia's Firmus, a data centre operator backed by Nvidia , shelved its $5 billion initial public offering on Friday, opting for a private fundraising round ahead of a potential New York share sale.
item.dc:creator: Scott Murdoch, Christine Chen
item.content:encoded: Australia's Firmus, a data centre operator backed by Nvidia (NVDA.O) , shelved its $5 billion initial public offering on Friday, opting for a private fundraising round ahead of a potential New York share sale. Firmus' IPO would have been the second-largest new share sale in Australia's history but met lukewarm demand, a warning sign that investors remain selective about AI issuers even as the artificial intelligence boom drives global markets. "The company will now pursue capital from private markets and consider alternative international public market options to support its next phase of growth," said co-founders Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield in a letter sent to shareholders and reviewed by Reuters. "We will continue to assess opportunities that provide the best platform to fund growth, create value and position Firmus for success." Firmus would aim to complete a Nasdaq listing after its next private fundraising round was finalised, a person involved in the transaction said. The person could not be named discussing information that was not public. The company declined to comment on whether it would target a Nasdaq listing. Firmus, backed by major AI companies and investors Nvidia and Coatue Management, along with Blackstone (BX.N) and Jane Street, designs and operates modular AI factories using proprietary energy and cooling technology. DATA CENTRE PARTNER'S EXIT SOWED DOUBTS Firmus [USN:L1N45N0G2 TEXT:"initially planned"] to sell its shares at A$11 each, giving it an equity valuation of $30.6 billion, nearly triple the $10.5 billion valuation it achieved following a fundraising [USN:L4N444084 TEXT:"round"] at the start of August. The pricing came under pressure as investors grew concerned about the company's debt pile, its lack of a track record in building AI data centres and media reports about a key partner pulling out of an A$73 billion data centre development deal. Firmus currently has two leased online data centres in Melbourne and Singapore and plans to build five more across the Asia-Pacific. Its [USN:L4N45F0GG TEXT:"draft prospectus"] said it would make $5 billion in annual earnings within five years from the data centres. "They were asking for a very big price tag for what would likely be expected to happen in the future assuming near flawless execution," said Joseph Koh, a portfolio manager at Blackwattle Investment Partners, who looked at the Firmus IPO but did not bid for stock. "And so I think the market wasn't comfortable taking that leap of faith quite at this stage yet," he said. The [USN:L1N45N0G2 TEXT:"term sheet"] sent when the deal was launched said indicative offers for the IPO were already enough to cover the transaction. Investors started to pull those orders on Wednesday, after CDC Data Centres CEO Greg Boorer told an Australian podcast Rampart its plan to develop 1.6 gigawatts of AI factories with Firmus was no longer underway, two people involved in the IPO said. Investors also balked after being told on Tuesday the deal's escrow arrangements would have allowed more than half the stock to be sold by existing investors from day one, which could have hurt Firmus' early trading performance. Firmus considered cutting the issue price to entice more investors, one of the people involved in the deal said, but opted instead to look towards a private funding round. The bookbuilding was led by Bank of America (BAC.N) , JPMorgan (JPM.N) , Morgan Stanley (MS.N) and Australian broker Morgans. VALUATION WORRIES With debt of about $30 billion, according to analysts working for the joint lead managers, the company founded in 2019 would have had an enterprise value of $60 billion, more than some of Australia's longest-established companies. Fund manager Ten Cap's co-founder Jun Bei Liu said the pulled Firmus deal showed a broader shift was taking place in which investors were becoming more focused on the economics of AI investments and converting infrastructure spending into returns. "I think the Firmus situation represents an important reality check for the AI investment boom, but I wouldn't interpret it as the beginning of the end of the AI trade," Liu said. "There are certainly Firmus-specific issues, particularly around the speed of its valuation increase, the enormous capital requirements and the execution risks associated with delivering its ambitious expansion plans." The world's largest technology companies, including Nvidia (NVDA.O) and SpaceX (SPCX.O) , are still busy [USN:L4N45T0NO TEXT:"tapping debt markets"] for tens of billions of dollars, while Anthropic is seeking to raise as much as $100 billion in an IPO. But in the latest sign of investors' concerns about returns from AI, US-listed chipmakers (.SOX) , which have soared over 80% so far this year, fell 3.4% on Thursday in the wake of a report from the Financial Times that OpenAI's annualised revenue was $20 billion less than the company previously signalled.

item.title: US to livestream Army firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
item.description: The US will livestream the Army's upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon said, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution.
item.dc:creator: Phil Stewart
item.content:encoded: The US will livestream the Army's upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon said, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution. Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by [USN:L1N45S037 TEXT:"firing squad"] by the US military since 1945. The execution is scheduled for December 3 at the same sprawling Texas base where Hasan opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility. It comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the [USN:L1N45M04O TEXT:"botched lethal injection"] of a Tennessee woman last week. "It will be livestreamed. Details will follow," a Pentagon official told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, confirmed plans to livestream the execution in an X post. Media have sought to televise US executions in the past but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream a legal execution, experts said. Public executions have become exceedingly rare worldwide. Among countries known to conduct them in recent years are Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan. Extrajudicial lynchings in the United States, often by white mobs targeting Black Americans, were public spectacles well into the 20th century. The last legally sanctioned public execution in the United States was conducted in 1936, death penalty experts said. Thousands watched that 1936 hanging of a young Black man who had been convicted of raping a white woman. Hegseth told the Human Events Daily program that deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1 p.m. — the approximate time, day of the week and location of the 2009 shooting — was a "no-brainer." "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public. Because people need to understand that ... there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3." PRESIDENT MUST APPROVE FIRING SQUAD EXECUTION A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder. The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest. Under US military law, a US president must approve an execution by firing squad. [USN:L1N45T015 TEXT:"President Donald Trump did so"] on Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon said on Monday. The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon. The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan's execution would be the first military execution since 1961. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the center reported. "It would be extremely, extremely strange" to livestream the event, said Eugene Fidell, a lawyer, author and military law expert who lectures at Yale Law School. While firing squads have a long history in American military law, as far as he knew it would be unprecedented to livestream or televise an execution, Fidell said, adding that Hasan would need to sue in federal court if he wanted to block a public display of his death. "The Supreme Court has never addressed this question, and it's an interesting question whether the current Supreme Court would put on their originalist hat and say, 'Well, it was OK in 1790, so what the hell?'" Fidell said. Jonathan Lurie, an author and historian of military justice, said there are no compelling reasons to make the execution public. "What's the point of it? Who would want to see that?" said Lurie. At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, [USN:L2N3PP0X8 TEXT:"South Carolina"] carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years. Death by firing squad is one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration[USN:L6N417125 TEXT:" recently added"] to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation. The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also sometimes proved challenging to carry out. Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched attempts to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalized. Her lawyers said on Wednesday she awoke "[USN:L1N45T0M9 TEXT:"angry and confused"]" in a hospital. Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, they said.

item.title: OpenAI's September annualized revenue nears $50 billion, less than previously indicated, source says
item.description: OpenAI has told investors its annualized revenue for September was almost $50 billion, a drop from what it signaled earlier, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Jaspreet Singh, Krystal Hu
item.content:encoded: OpenAI has told investors its annualized revenue for September was almost $50 billion, a drop from what it signaled earlier, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday. The company previously indicated to investors at a separate event that its revenue run rate for last month was [USN:L4N45L1EC TEXT:"approaching $70 billion"], Reuters and other media reported. The discrepancy mainly arose from an attempt to produce a direct comparison with figures from rival Anthropic, the person said on condition of anonymity. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. The latest revenue figure was first reported by the Financial Times. OpenAI, unlike Anthropic, does not include, for instance, revenue from sales via cloud partners such as Amazon's (AMZN.O) AWS and Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google Cloud. Anthropic pays cloud partners [USN:L6N45K15A TEXT:"about 16% of every dollar"] earned through them, which last year accounted for half of revenue, a Reuters analysis showed. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing to go public, a process through which Wall Street is likely to gain a clearer view of finances, including the sustainability of rapid revenue growth brought about by a boom in demand for AI applications. OpenAI started this year with $20 billion in annualized revenue versus $6 billion in 2024. Its quarterly revenue was eclipsed by Anthropic for the first time in the second quarter, with OpenAI reporting $6.7 billion compared to Anthropic's $11.5 billion. Anthropic's annualized revenue crossed $65 billion in July, and is set to reach $100 billion by year-end, sources previously told Reuters. Analysts consider annualized revenue run rate a sometimes misleading sales metric, which often involves multiplying one month's revenue by 12. It has nonetheless become a popular metric among fast-growing Silicon Valley startups.

item.title: The skilled foreign tech workers' green card program under attack from Trump
item.description: Some experts say such policies risk making the US less competitive globally by deterring highly skilled foreign talent.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Sophia, Jaspreet Singh
item.content:encoded: The US government said on Thursday it is [USN:L6N45U111 TEXT:"suspending"] some of the world's biggest tech and IT firms including Microsoft, Cognizant and Capgemini from a key green card program that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency through their employment. Senior US officials cited alleged fraud as the reason behind the move, saying companies have been using the program to replace American workers with cheaper foreign workers, and comes as the latest step in the Trump administration's crackdown on skilled foreign labor. WHAT IS UNDER SUSPENSION? The suspension is targeting a key employer-sponsorship mechanism, called the Permanent Labor Certification or PERM, which is used by major technology companies and outsourcing firms. The US government said that for certain companies, it would not accept any new PERM applications or process any pending ones. PERM came into effect in 2005, aiming to speed up the long processing times experienced under the previous paper-based "Alien Employment Certification" program. Under the program, the US Department of Labor (DOL) allows an employer to sponsor a foreign worker permanent residency. The process is initiated by qualified US employers, and not individual workers. The Labor Department must certify to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services that there are not enough US workers that are qualified and available for a given job opportunity, and that the employment of the foreign worker will not affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed Americans. Outside of PERM and family-based routes to permanent residency, individuals can also self-petition for green cards through processes such as the EB-1A application for individuals with extraordinary ability or the EB-2 National Interest Waiver. WHY IS IT IMPORTANT? The PERM program serves as a critical bridge between temporary work status and a green card for many foreign skilled workers. Many IT firms employ hundreds of thousands of workers who typically start on temporary work visas such as the H-1B, and later seek permanent residency. Without the option to be sponsored by their employer under PERM, foreign workers could lose a key route to permanent residency and would have to stay on temporary visas for longer. For companies, recruiting foreign talent could become harder, as many workers overseas view the path to permanent US residency as a key reason for taking a job. WHICH COMPANIES ARE UNDER SUSPENSION? The US said it is suspending Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Adobe (ADBE.O) along with some of the largest IT firms in the world, including Cognizant (CTSH.O) , Infosys (INFY.NS) , Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) , Wipro (WIPR.NS) , HCL Technologies (HCLT.NS) and Capgemini (CAPP.PA) . Other companies such as Meta (META.O) , Amazon (AMZN.O) or Alphabet's Google (GOOGL.O) remain free to participate in the program. WHY IS THE US FREEZING APPLICATIONS? The move widens an ongoing crackdown on visas which the Trump administration has said cost US jobs. Vice President JD Vance said, without citing specific evidence, companies are using the PERM program to replace American employees with foreign workers and undercut their wages. Vance said on Thursday: "Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers." The suspensions follow President Trump's move to impose a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions for highly skilled foreign workers, which has been blocked by federal court orders. HOW IS PERM DIFFERENT FROM H-1B? H-1B is a temporary work visa that allows skilled foreign workers to work in the US, generally for up to six years. PERM meanwhile is a permanent labor-certification process. The freeze does not appear to directly affect current holders of H-1B visas. HOW CURTAILING PERM COULD BACKFIRE Some experts said that while the PERM suspensions might target specific companies, such policies risk making the US less competitive globally by deterring highly skilled foreign talent. "It is a fallacy to think that you can protect American workers by keeping skilled foreign workers out of the country. You think that foreign talent competes with Americans within our borders, they'll certainly compete with Americans by working abroad," said Chad Sparber, Director of the Lampert Institute for Civic and Global Affairs at Colgate University. Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford’s Immigration Policy Lab, said that permanent residency is the primary way for talented foreign workers to stay in the country and without it, some will leave, and some will not come in the first place, even temporarily.

item.title: Trump says US will not attack Iran before midterm elections in November
item.description: President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm congressional elections, asserting that the two countries are having "productive" talks about ending the six-month-old war.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm congressional elections , asserting that the two countries are having "productive" talks about ending the six-month-old war. "We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd." The war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump's domestic approval ratings downward and is weighing heavily on his fellow Republicans as they seek to preserve their narrow legislative majorities in November's election. Some 60% of Americans — including one in four Republicans — disapprove of how Trump is handling the situation in Iran, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The conflict has pushed gasoline prices sharply higher at a time when voters say their top concern is the cost of living. Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but he has not offered a detailed plan for exiting the war. Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer. Iran's state media reported on Thursday that Tehran would not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium stockpile, citing the head of the country's Atomic Energy Organization, days after US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make "[USN:L1N45T0DK TEXT:"meaningful" reductions"] in its enrichment capacity. The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied.

item.title: Shell partially restarts Pearl gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar
item.description: Shell said on Thursday it had partially restarted its Pearl gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar, as traders said QatarEnergy returned Pearl-GTL naphtha cargoes to the spot market six months after the facility was damaged during the Iran war.
item.dc:creator: Mohi Narayan, Stephanie Kelly, Shadia Nasralla
item.content:encoded: Shell (SHEL.L) said on Thursday it had partially restarted its Pearl gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar, as traders said QatarEnergy returned Pearl-GTL naphtha cargoes to the spot market six months after the facility was damaged during the Iran war. Shell said the move would allow it to build a limited amount of product inventory in storage, while its ability to ship product remains subject to the regional security situation. QatarEnergy has begun offering cargoes that include Pearl-GTL naphtha and resumed some contractual deliveries, signalling some return of products from the facility to a supply-starved market. The war disrupted refinery operations and temporarily shut the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20% of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies previously passed. Several traders who participate in the market said QatarEnergy issued a spot tender offering up to 50,000 metric tons of naphtha f four grades including Pearl GTL on a free-on-board basis from Ras Laffan port inside the Strait of Hormuz. The state-owned refiner's last naphtha tender, which also included Pearl GTL grade, was awarded at a discount of $150 to Middle East quotes on FOB basis. It [USN:L4N45R0QO TEXT:"has resumed"] sending contract volumes of naphtha to some buyers. India's Haldia Petrochemicals received its 50,000 metric tons for this quarter, a company executive said on Monday. Shell did not comment on the market tender and QatarEnergy did not respond to a request for comment. Oil companies typically do not comment on tenders. REPAIRS TO TRAIN 2 EXPECTED IN Q1 2027 Shell's wholly owned Pearl, which is fed from Qatar's North gas field, was [USN:L6N4070VH TEXT:"hit"] in March, damaging one of its two processing plants, also known as trains. At full capacity, Pearl can produce 140,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. Pearl's output also feeds into Shell's downstream supply chain, including its lubricants business. Repairs to the facility's Train 2 are expected to be completed in the first quarter of next year, a Shell spokesperson said. Shell estimated in March that it would take one year to fully repair Pearl. Shell said its ability to sustain safe and reliable operations at Pearl depends on regional security, including the safe passage of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The first LNG train under QatarEnergy's North Field East expansion project [USN:L1N45T0GE TEXT:"will be ready"] to start operation in November, two people aware of its plans said, offering Qatar a path to restoring some lost output.

item.title: Trump administration freezes green cards for Microsoft, IT firms, probes universities
item.description: The US suspended Microsoft , major IT outsourcers and software maker Adobe from a key green-card program on Thursday while opening probes into nine top universities, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: The US suspended Microsoft (MSFT.O) , major IT outsourcers and software maker Adobe (ADBE.O) from a key green-card program on Thursday while opening probes into nine top universities, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs. Since taking office, US President Donald Trump has pursued a broad effort to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship. Thursday's twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs — potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers — while putting some of the country's top research universities on notice. "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft," Vice President JD Vance said. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. His comments came hours before Trump honored tech billionaires for their contributions to America, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. Nadella once held an H-1B visa, as did Elon Musk, who was also honored, while three of the other CEOs honored are immigrants. Nadella thanked Trump for the medal, saying in a post on X he would continue to advance technology and drive American prosperity. Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, or the [USN:L4N45U1DA TEXT:"permanent labor certification"] process, according to data from the US labor department. Under PERM, which most employment-based green cards require, employers must show a foreign hire will not hurt US workers' wages or jobs. The company said in a statement that about 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would [USN:L4N4380XC TEXT:"cut 4,800 jobs"], or about 2.1% of its global workforce. CRACKDOWN WIDENS Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant (CTSH.O) , Infosys (INFY.NS) , Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) , Wipro (WIPR.NS) , HCL Technologies (HCLT.NS) and Capgemini (CAPP.PA) . "We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said. He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to US immigration data. Vance said the suspensions would last "as long as it needs to," and that the administration wanted the companies to change how they hire. He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then point to the lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work. Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment. Nasscom, India's IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process. In September last year, the Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called "Project Firewall" as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad. UNIVERSITIES UNDER SCRUTINY Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages. The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. D'Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research. “It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent $40 billion a year while in the US, she said. The probe deepens the administration's [USN:L1N45M14M TEXT:"long-running fight"] with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law. Harvard called that subpoena "unfounded retribution" but said it would comply as far as the law requires. Rapidly changing visa policies caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its journalism programs, Reuters reported last week.

item.title: Plane damaged at Riyadh airport as Houthis escalate attacks, sources say
item.description: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, trying to shut down the kingdom's airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that has killed three people this week and left a plane badly damaged.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, trying to shut down the kingdom's airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that has killed three people this week and left a plane badly damaged. The group said it had struck Riyadh airport and warned workers to stay away from energy plants, which would be targeted. Shrapnel from an interception or another projectile hit had left the commercial plane belonging to Saudi state carrier Saudia Airlines heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at an airport terminal on Thursday, three people briefed on the matter said. They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the time but they could not rule out any injuries as a result of the incident. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from Riyadh airport in video verified by Reuters. Saudi Arabia's government media office, its civil aviation authority and Saudia Airlines did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Lufthansa and Air India said they were [USN:L6N45U10R TEXT:"suspending "]flights to Riyadh after Houthi attacks. Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh. The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen's reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen's UN-recognised government to take back territory from the Houthis. The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war , has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into gruelling mountain fighting, with Syria now considering [USN:L1N45U05X TEXT:"deploying troops"] to assist Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including [USN:L6N45T0IX TEXT:"Turkey"] and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been [USN:L1N45T00S TEXT:"killed"] this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport in the southwest. DELAYS AND CANCELLATIONS The Houthis have made Saudi airports a focus of their strikes, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it had destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the group towards Riyadh and another towards Khamis Mushayt, home to a major airbase. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from Riyadh airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports. Flight tracker FlightRadar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday. The airport advised travellers to contact airlines to check the status of flights before trying to travel. Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policy makers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week. Several multinational firms based in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after loud booms were heard on Thursday morning, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment. Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms. CIVIL WAR REIGNITED BY CONFLICT IN IRAN Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Their threats to shipping and attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure have drawn the kingdom back in. This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a [USN:L8N45M1W0 TEXT:"counterattack"], taking back some areas around the strait. However, in a war with several front lines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden. The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of [USN:L6N45S0PX TEXT:"Saudi-backed forces"] under the internationally recognised government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed. One US and one Syrian defence official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight to the Houthis. In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war. NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.

item.title: French students keep up protest pressure with some demonstrations hit by violence
item.description: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday in the latest wave of nationwide protests about conditions in the country's schools, and some of the demonstrations were marred by violent unrest.
item.dc:creator: Manon Cruz, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday in the latest wave of nationwide protests about conditions in the country's schools, and some of the demonstrations were marred by violent unrest. The Interior Ministry said 71,500 people participated in the day's demonstrations, of which 24,500 took part in the main Paris protest centred around the Bastille square. The Paris protest was mostly peaceful, although there were occasional clashes between small groups of demonstrators and the police during the evening. Elsewhere, arsonists attacked a [USN:FWN45U1T1 TEXT:"Bordeaux"] police station, a school in Saint-Etienne was ransacked and a teacher in Toulouse was hit by a demonstrator, said the Interior Ministry. In Marseille, police said a teacher at Victor Hugo High School [USN:FWN45U1T4 TEXT:"was attacked"] during the latest protests and has filed a criminal complaint over the incident. A banner reads: "Funding cut, youth sacrificed." REUTERS/Manon Cruz The protest movement, now into its third week, has exposed deep tensions in France between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and a cash-strapped government under [USN:L8N45S1P0 TEXT:"pressure from bond markets"] to reduce its debt and deficit. Protesters say they are demonstrating to demand more teachers and better facilities, arguing school buildings are often dilapidated, with overcrowded classrooms that are often freezing in winter and boiling in summer. Critics say the movement has been infiltrated by violent far-left and anarchist elements. High-school teacher Diane Di Sciullo joined students in Marseille, saying all they were asking for was a decent education in decent conditions. She denounced overcrowding, saying this year she had 37 students in her class. "At the start of every lesson, I have to ask them to check the neighbouring classrooms for spare chairs and desks so they can actually study," she said. Di Sciullo, 28, was carrying a placard that read, "I'm a teacher and my students help me catch cockroaches in class." MINISTER PROMISES URGENT ACTION Education ministry figures showed the number of school blockades was gradually decreasing. Education Minister Edouard Geffray told TF1 TV that extra teachers would be drafted in to plug gaps in schools which do not have enough teachers, while heavy school timetables will also be reviewed. It is not uncommon for French teenagers to have lessons from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., as well as large amounts of homework. Geffray also said he was working on potential improvements to Parcoursup, the national online portal for applying to university, which has been widely criticised as confusing and stressful for applicants. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu pledged late on Wednesday that the government would present "concrete, quick and fully funded responses" to the protests by late October, without offering specifics. Student protest leaders said that was not good enough and called for further marches next Tuesday. There are also calls circulating online for a day of protests on October 17. "Our demands must be heard. Yesterday, Mr Lecornu gave us a lot of hot air," said Ryad Rani, leader of one of the student unions. "The mobilisation will continue, we're not backing down on anything." A prominent complaint featured on banners and placards was that the police response to the wave of protests has been too heavy-handed. "Too young to be listened to, old enough to be tear-gassed" was one example. There have been hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries since the movement started. On Wednesday, the government [USN:L1N45T0EM TEXT:"suspended the use of stun grenades"] in the policing of the protests after one [USN:L1N45R08Q TEXT:"teenager's hand was blown off"]. POLITICAL RESPONSE SHOWS POLARISATION AS ELECTION LOOMS Six months from a presidential election, the protests have highlighted stark polarisation between leading candidates to replace Emmanuel Macron, who cannot seek a third term. Far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen has highlighted damage to schools caused by a minority of protesters and outlined [USN:L8N45R1J6 TEXT:"plans to slash public spending"] should she win. Her hard-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon, who also has a chance of making the runoff, has praised the protesters as "incredible" and denounced police brutality. According to an Elabe poll for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students' demands are legitimate, but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Neighbouring [USN:L1N45T0NH TEXT:"Belgium"] has also had student protests, with demonstrations in Brussels, Ciney and Liege.

item.title: AirBaltic plans to cut up to 700 jobs (Oct. 5)
item.description: Latvian airline airBaltic said on Monday it is preparing to cut about 500 to 700 jobs across its bases in Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Latvian airline airBaltic said on Monday it is preparing to cut about 500 to 700 jobs across its bases in Riga, Vilnius and Tallinn. The carrier [USN:L6N4560BC TEXT:"filed"] for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in New York in September, aiming to complete a sweeping restructuring focused on cutting its mounting debt through capacity and fleet reductions AirBaltic gained [USN:L6N4580GU TEXT:"approval last month"] to access €140 million ($157 million) from a wider €350 million financing package. CEO Erno Hilden told Reuters in September that the airline [USN:L6N456122 TEXT:"was in talks"] with labour unions over "an adjustment" to the workforce New organisational structures for the rest of the company are expected to be defined by mid-October, airBaltic said, with the final number of layoffs potentially changing within the course of the process Dace Kavasa, chairperson of the Latvian aviation union, told Reuters the announcement could be seen as "pure union busting" as the airline did not disclose the potential number of layoffs with unions before making it public "We learned about 500 to 700 people, six minutes before they started an employee meeting where they presented this," Kavasa said, adding that any talks will only start on October 15 Unions have proposed staff to take 85% part-time work and are pushing towards offering 50%, Kavasa added ($1 = 0.8922 euros)

item.content:encoded: L'Europe vue dans le vert, accalmie sur le pétrole et les rendements 9 octobre (Reuters) - Les principales Bourses européennes sont attendues sur un rebond vendredi à l'ouverture, portées par la baisse des cours du pétrole et une accalmie sur le marché obligataire, même si la volatilité reste élevée en raison des craintes budgétaires dans des pays comme la France. Le secteur du luxe freiné davantage par des mesures fiscales en Chine PARIS/PEKIN, 9 octobre (Reuters) - Le tour de vis enclenché par la Chine pour lutter contre l'évasion fiscale des plus fortunés est devenu un motif supplémentaire d'inquiétude pour les enseignes de luxe, lesquelles font déjà face aux répercussions de la guerre en Iran et à un ralentissement de la consommation aux Etats-Unis. Le gouvernement allemand relève ses prévisions de croissance pour 2026 et 2027 BERLIN, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Le gouvernement allemand a revu à la hausse ses prévisions économiques pour cette année et l'année prochaine, la guerre en Iran n'ayant pas un impact aussi sévère qu'initialement redouté, a déclaré jeudi le ministère de l'Economie. Zone euro: Les rendements obligataires se tendent encore LONDRES, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les rendements obligataires de la zone euro enregistrent jeudi de nouvelles fortes tensions, dans un contexte de hausse des prix de l'énergie, les investisseurs continuant à se débarrasser des obligations des pays les plus endettés comme la France et l'Italie, provoquant un creusement des "spreads" dans le bloc. Aux yeux du patron de Ryanair, le coût du kérosène restera élevé une année de plus BRUXELLES/LONDRES, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les compagnies aériennes européennes vont connaître une nouvelle année de coûts de carburant élevés et de taris en hausse, la guerre en Iran maintenant les prix du kérosène à un niveau supérieur d'environ 50% à celui d'avant le conflit, a déclaré jeudi Michael O'Leary, directeur général de Ryanair. Le choc géopolitique se répercute désormais sur les marchés financiers, selon Moulin (BCE) FRANCFORT, 8 octobre (Reuters) - La quasi-totalité du choc inflationniste subi par l'Europe cette année est liée à l'énergie, mais les chocs géopolitiques à l'origine de la flambée des prix "se traduisent désormais par un choc financier", a déclaré jeudi Emmanuel Moulin, gouverneur de la Banque de France (BdF) et membre de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE). BCE-Wunsch contre un relèvement du ratio de réserves obligatoires des banques FRANCFORT, 8 octobre (Reuters) - La projet de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE) visant à relever le ratio de réserves obligatoires imposé aux banques commerciales pourrait nuire à la crédibilité de ses futures opérations, voire empiéter sur la politique budgétaire des Etats, a déclaré jeudi Pierre Wunsch, membre du Conseil des gouverneurs de l'institution de Francfort et gouverneur de la Banque nationale de Belgique. Allemagne: Baisse surprise des exportations en août 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les exportations allemandes ont baissé de façon inattendue en août, accusant un recul de 0,8% par rapport au mois précédent, selon les données de l'Office fédéral de la statistique publiées jeudi. PepsiCo revoit à la baisse de ses prévisions, annonce de nouvelles réductions des coûts 8 octobre (Reuters) - PepsiCo a annoncé jeudi son intention de mettre en œuvre de nouvelles mesures de réduction des coûts après avoir revu à la baisse ses prévisions de bénéfice annuel récurrent, en raison d'une demande atone pour ses snacks et ses boissons en Amérique du Nord et de la hausse des coûts des matières premières.
